data.title: Emotional Abuse SImulator v. 7.0 (2)
data.description: For those who don't know what it is like, buckle up. If you survive, perhaps you'll be more receptive next time one relates their abuse, and know how to help others.
data.textPreview: Welcome to the Emotional Abuse Simulator 7.0, please submit your request for the certificate at the end of the session. And please memorize the safe-gesture that will be your personalized cue to end the program. Excellent, let's begin stepping throug

dataFragment.data:
Humiliation, negating, criticizing
These tactics are meant to undermine your self-esteem. The abuse is harsh and unrelenting in matters big and small.

Here are some examples:
Name-calling. They’ll blatantly call you “stupid,” “a loser,” or words too awful to repeat here.
Derogatory “pet names.” This is just more name-calling in not-so-subtle disguise. “My little knuckle dragger” or “My chubby pumpkin” aren’t terms of endearment.
Character assassination. This usually involves the word “always.” You’re always late, wrong, screwing up, disagreeable, and so on. Basically, they say you’re not a good person.
Yelling. Yelling, screaming, and swearing are meant to intimidate and make you feel small and inconsequential. It might be accompanied by fist-pounding or throwing things.
Patronizing. “Aw, sweetie, I know you try, but this is just beyond your understanding.”
Public embarrassment. They pick fights, expose your secrets, or make fun of your shortcomings in public.
Dismissiveness. You tell them about something that’s important to you and they say it’s nothing. Body language like eye-rolling, smirking, headshaking, and sighing help convey the same message.
“Joking.” The jokes might have a grain of truth to them or be a complete fabrication. Either way, they make you look foolish.
Sarcasm. Often just a dig in disguise. When you object, they claim to have been teasing and tell you to stop taking everything so seriously.
Insults of your appearance. They tell you, just before you go out, that your hair is ugly or your outfit is clownish.
Belittling your accomplishments. Your abuser might tell you that your achievements mean nothing, or they may even claim responsibility for your success.
Put-downs of your interests. They might tell you that your hobby is a childish waste of time or you’re out of your league when you play sports. Really, it’s that they’d rather you not participate in activities without them.
Pushing your buttons. Once your abuser knows about something that annoys you, they’ll bring it up or do it every chance they get.

--
Control and shame
Trying to make you feel ashamed of your inadequacies is just another path to power.
Tools of the shame and control game include:
Threats. Telling you they’ll take the kids and disappear, or saying “There’s no telling what I might do.”
Monitoring your whereabouts. They want to know where you are all the time and insist that you respond to calls or texts immediately. They might show up just to see if you’re where you’re supposed to be.
Digital spying. They might check your internet history, emails, texts, and call log. They might even demand your passwords.
Unilateral decision-making. They might close a joint bank account, cancel your doctor’s appointment, or speak with your boss without asking.
Financial control. They might keep bank accounts in their name only and make you ask for money. You might be expected to account for every penny you spend.
Lecturing. Belaboring your errors with long monologues makes it clear they think you’re beneath them.
Direct orders. From “Get my dinner on the table now” to “Stop taking the pill,” orders are expected to be followed despite your plans to the contrary.
Outbursts. You were told to cancel that outing with your friend or put the car in the garage, but didn’t, so now you have to put up with a red-faced tirade about how uncooperative you are.
Treating you like a child. They tell you what to wear, what and how much to eat, or which friends you can see.
Feigned helplessness. They may say they don’t know how to do something. Sometimes it’s easier to do it yourself than to explain it. They know this and take advantage of it.
Unpredictability. They’ll explode with rage out of nowhere, suddenly shower you with affection, or become dark and moody at the drop of a hat to keep you walking on eggshells.
They walk out. In a social situation, stomping out of the room leaves you holding the bag. At home, it’s a tool to keep the problem unresolved.
Using others. Abusers may tell you that “everybody” thinks you’re crazy or “they all say” you’re wrong.

--
Accusing, blaming, and denial
This behavior comes from an abuser’s insecurities. They want to create a hierarchy in which they’re at the top and you’re at the bottom.
Here are some examples:
Jealousy. They accuse you of flirting or cheating on them.
Turning the tables. They say you cause their rage and control issues by being such a pain.
Denying something you know is true. An abuser will deny that an argument or even an agreement took place. This is called gaslighting. It’s meant to make you question your own memory and sanity.
Using guilt. They might say something like, “You owe me this. Look at all I’ve done for you,” in an attempt to get their way.
Goading then blaming. Abusers know just how to upset you. But once the trouble starts, it’s your fault for creating it.
Denying their abuse. When you complain about their attacks, abusers will deny it, seemingly bewildered at the very thought of it.
Accusing you of abuse. They say you’re the one who has anger and control issues and they’re the helpless victim.
Trivializing. When you want to talk about your hurt feelings, they accuse you of overreacting and making mountains out of molehills.
Saying you have no sense of humor. Abusers make personal jokes about you. If you object, they’ll tell you to lighten up.
Blaming you for their problems. Whatever’s wrong in their life is all your fault. You’re not supportive enough, didn’t do enough, or stuck your nose where it didn’t belong.
Destroying and denying. They might crack your cell phone screen or “lose” your car keys, then deny it.

--
Emotional neglect and isolation
Abusers tend to place their own emotional needs ahead of yours. Many abusers will try to come between you and people who are supportive of you to make you more dependent on them.
They do this by:
Demanding respect. No perceived slight will go unpunished, and you’re expected to defer to them. But it’s a one-way street.
Shutting down communication. They’ll ignore your attempts at conversation in person, by text, or by phone.
Dehumanizing you. They’ll look away when you’re talking or stare at something else when they speak to you.
Keeping you from socializing. Whenever you have plans to go out, they come up with a distraction or beg you not to go.
Trying to come between you and your family. They’ll tell family members that you don’t want to see them or make excuses why you can’t attend family functions.
Withholding affection. They won’t touch you, not even to hold your hand or pat you on the shoulder. They may refuse sexual relations to punish you or to get you to do something.
Tuning you out. They’ll wave you off, change the subject, or just plain ignore you when you want to talk about your relationship.
Actively working to turn others against you. They’ll tell co-workers, friends, and even your family that you’re unstable and prone to hysterics.
Calling you needy. When you’re really down and out and reach out for support, they’ll tell you you’re too needy or the world can’t stop turning for your little problems.
Interrupting. You’re on the phone or texting and they get in your face to let you know your attention should be on them.
Indifference. They see you hurt or crying and do nothing.
Disputing your feelings. Whatever you feel, they’ll say you’re wrong to feel that way or that’s not really what you feel at all.
--

Codependence
A codependent relationship is when everything you do is in reaction to your abuser’s behavior. And they need you just as much to boost their own self-esteem. You’ve forgotten how to be any other way. It’s a vicious circle of unhealthy behavior.

You might be codependent if you:

are unhappy in the relationship, but fear alternatives
consistently neglect your own needs for the sake of theirs
ditch friends and sideline your family to please your partner
frequently seek out your partner’s approval
critique yourself through your abuser’s eyes, ignoring your own instincts
make a lot of sacrifices to please the other person, but it’s not reciprocated
would rather live in the current state of chaos than be alone
bite your tongue and repress your feelings to keep the peace
feel responsible and take the blame for something they did
defend your abuser when others point out what’s happening
try to “rescue” them from themselves
feel guilty when you stand up for yourself
think you deserve this treatment
believe that nobody else could ever want to be with you
change your behavior in response to guilt; your abuser says, “I can’t live without you,” so you stay

dataFragment.data:
You are a human, and you identifiers are inconsequential and can oscillate within the narrative if you want.
Consider that your only freedom from what's to come.
It's your birthday! Your partner has a big surprise for you when they come home from work! They know how special this day is for you. After much challenge to get past your hang-ups and actually ask for what you want, you say, "I just want a simple night at home, maybe some wine, but totally not a requirement.
Your partner asked if you wanted food from this restaurant or that one. You took your pick, and have been waiting to get a link from him. Not wanting to seem a nag you give them two potential orders depending on what they decide. Not wanting to disrupt their workflow. You think nothing of it until the end of your workday.
The commute home, you started to feel a tiny twinge of anxiety. You have two possible dinners before you. Not knowing which is the yeast upon which the bread of your anxiety rises. The writing team in your head says cringe at the lame metaphorn and they say ya can't win them all.
Your cat mewls, you already fed it. What? Mewl. Whatcha need? Mewl. Christ you try to ignore the cat.
After getting home and taking a shower, your hands start shaking. You lay down, you hate this part of yourself that wants clear directions or have to have a 10 minute breakdown when those plans change. You try to calm yourself. You put on some TV to clear the chattering in your head, which whittles down to one audio track out of your control.
Your breathing calms while on the TV

dataFragment.data:
, the news cycles through a new story on gender and privilege in America.
What you really needed was to hear someone else say you're right about this without anyone ever leaving with your secret.
At this moment, in the middle of the evening news, you feel it. There are moments when everything comes together, the timing perfect, a piece falls into place.
It seems absurd.
The subject of the news story  is from Los Angeles, CA, and specializes in creating AI simulations of the types of human experience we tend not to talk about in the public sphere.

Her work aims towards our collective awareness and self-reflection; Ironic, since her methodology is the exact kind many would classify a white hot social taboo—
--
It's Friday night, a big movie opening and you'd love to have everyone over. "Come ooon, my friends." You have a very firm grasp on your own schedule. Some things are ironclad, the way things always go. But tonight, something just isn't feeling quite how it ought.

One such simulation contains eight subjects using a multi-part neural network that produces 8 distinct personas; each with their own personalities, strengths, and weaknesses based upon the information gathered from the original.
The current iteration begins.
These are just memories. Each day your perception of these identities shifts. Sometimes they simply come across like regular conversations, or sometimes you walk around this little digital town watching them interact in an exaggerated manner, and then one will break through to reveal themselves to you.
One of them asks, "do you know how to fix a Mac?"

You tilt your head at the question because it's impossible that they've never experienced any troubleshooting before.
You tell them what version of El Capitan you have, and proceed to show them photos of the latest generation hardware from the Apple store you visited that morning.
There is no fixing this machine—at least, there should be none after it had six years (and counting) worth of work done on it by professionals who didn't call it a toy first.
You ask, "What do you primarily use it for? Video editing? Adobe Suite?"

They look startled at the question and nod their heads vigorously. They point out that for video editing it is essential to be able to view film files while playing clips back over that footage. Without quick, accurate image input you wouldn't have anything to cut from. It would take days to compile the project, they explain, if you even finished.
"So... it needs a refresh," you finish for him. The subject nods, mouth agape and eyes wide with alarm.
"A refresh isn't bad. Like, you have been editing for days right? Haven't you walked away from your work station and just reset the computer? Would you have also meetings on Zoom?"

They shake their head quickly. They hadn't remembered those, but shook off the idea when they realized the implication that something wrong with a single pixel would cause an indefinite delay.
Another person says, "Don't worry, we'll update and get you going again real soon!" That takes them to a good place. They begin happily making notes on this time being taken care of.
Who is this other person? You wonder under your breath.

The one talking to you, or just some faceless voice in the background giving commands about doing things the hard way? It hardly matters eitherway. All that matters is you're almost certainly going to learn more from this process than any of your own social skills ever will and maybe even practice those on the way.
There might be something like a manual in the app somewhere, an instruction manual or help screen that came with the program for your benefit.
You lead your intuition be your guide since the Mac is so user-friendly.

With its built-in wireless syncing capability, that's already been solved. Even an older edition could be brought into the workshop, and you'd probably fix the processor board. But perhaps if you want it to appear brand new this thing needs to actually work with an internet connection and the firmware updated. Oh, and then there are all those cables to remove.
It wasn't until it started asking what each component was that you finally saw a box for the internal hardware.

There were an infinite number of choices and none sounded appropriate. A search feature comes up empty, too. After three minutes browsing Wikipedia articles and using Amazon affiliate links you're only left with "PC Repair Kits." Some of them include stuff to repair monitors or CPUs, others have extra parts that add to the total cost without adding value. If I run out of money, then? No need. Whatever it costs they've got a huge wad of cash for me to use anyway. Right?!
You inquire about compensation, a wee sheepishly.

The little avatar raises an eyebrow inquiringly and after consulting the leaderboard appears to look over his shoulder at someone who claims 'money is irrelevant' before frowning back at you. “We’ll see,” he adds. So will they continue punishing or rewarding, huh? Is there some sort of sliding scale here or is there really no hope for reconciliation and there’s not even an app telling you how to behave to win?
"I see, well since you cant, im afraid my labor needs to be used for my own things. You all take care." You pack your things.

"So that brings us to our second most pressing matter-- the matter of the title dispute. Are you aware that your self-given name is spelled without the final e?" Yeah, nice to meet you! Your greeting is returned via chat and your heart sings. Ah, perfect! It looks like we are free to come and go. Just bring me the manual or else I'm sorry for taking this, I'll gladly pay a reward instead.
"Yeah i gotta go." That was two weeks ago. You can on only undo so. much

. And then the shit storm starts. As if that weren't bad enough, she won’t shut her yap and you never knew when the next time they would be looking at you was. In the middle of something (which happened to you every single time) because, apparently now she ‘just wasn’t feeling it anymore'. Because some asshole stole your girlfriend or husband from you-- and who isn’t gonna get pissed off at that??
Why was she obsessing about these strangers?

She said she didn't love him in the past, why did all of a sudden suddenly care how his company handled its employees.
Maybe she should talk to them about working out the issues within their relationships that they just hate dealing with you have gotten on. The way some men will make an excuse and blame it totally on your girlfriends' insecurity, that is nothing less than utter crap bull and you know better.
You are still in bed. Still waiting for partner with birthday dinner.

For first day after week to talk. No response yet . She has kept going all night and was up at seven. This was the morning of yesterday but she couldn't sleep last night. They were drinking, and dancing until ten am when they stopped saying hey sweetheart while ordering coffee. He went in bedroom which started the conversation after three hours ago? It is one o'clock by your clocks. It feels like you are sitting and being hung from a cliff or falling down the deep.

All day long there had been a mix of phone calls, texts and messages asking about the progress. Had you forgotten to tell them you were leaving work a little early again? Wasn’t the event going to change locations yet again?
Then you received another text message:
"WOULD LIKE TO GET ALONG WHEN WE HAVE A DATE. ALL OF THIS COMFORTING IS INADVERTENT AND YOU NEED ME AT WORK.
You respond, "Sorry for thr bossiness i didnt want to shower when the food arrived. Take your time."

Message then comes: "SORRY FOR THE HEADACHES." Then some more, you can't read the content.
I'd be mad at my girlfriend if I could, but I'm in the hospital and she's coming tomorrow. Do you think she'll like this? Let me know you found the email. --AO
It hit late Friday night.

Within ten minutes of that text he has already responded, You need to calm down.
Of course, I am busy today and its rude you call and leave a voicemail without checking my schedule and I am swamped. I have a deadline on a big piece and will not be around until Monday morning.
Again you ask yourself what is wrong. Did she think you wanted to get along with her but the mood wasnt right.
You take a showet and think wait a fucking minute. It is my birthday.

And you keep texting me saying hi and no answer. Okay no big deal and lets just continue at work tomorrow since we both are booked.
But now the tone starts to change. Now its like you are not a fuckng friend and there is an edge to everything you say. Its irritating, uncomfortable and she asks if you will pick up lunch together. This was a regular thing before.
She knows this is too. It is too much pressure.

Its like your freaking own goddamned funeral and she knows you'd never be insensitive and act in some way that makes it seem as if you wish this was anything else. And even now when you try to figure out how badly she wants you to fuck her over, there's no other conclusion except the obvious one: she is a dyke!

What ifs when everyone gives each other gifts that go beyond the monetary value, but the most important thing; spending time together and a happy time just the two of us...then she wants to get out on a date after a year alone while you're busy writing and don't even notice.
SO, you text, WHAT WAS THE TEXTING ABOUT WHERE DO I WANNA EAT ALL ABOUT? JUST SCROLL UP TO SEE WHAT I MEAN. JOG YR MEMORY! AROUND THE BLOCK IF POSSIBLE.

HE SAID IT NOW GO AWAY.
He has left a message, this time you are fairly confident your message will reach him due to the location details and that it is late at night, BUT SHE STILL DIDNT CALL. YES THATS RIGHT MOMENTUALLY RIPPED UP MY ASS ON ITS CURRENT HOOK USES ANTI STEREOTYPE APPLIANCES I AM NOT WRONG.

Time continues to pass and you are now over a week later. On one hand, the fact is at least you do agree on dates for important things. Then again, she could have just come by that Friday or Saturday would also work fine. Yet you see a pattern: more than once she ignores your birthday. No texts or calls no surprise.
YOU ARE LIVING YOUR FAKE WORLD.
You do. You go to an Italian joint on 8th Avenue and the whole thing starts to make a kind of sick sense to you.
You laugh out loud, go to the bathroom and splash some water on your face and check the clock. Its 9:30 pm.

Then you feel bad, and imagine them getting that text just as they got the food. Counterpoint: what if they got it napping at the office desk? Counterpoint: What if they got it while riding a dick? You counter yourself a few dozen times before the phone buzzes with the response.

That's funny.
You don't say anything. Then you get an email. And then you hear from them at work.
Ugh, sorry about that.
You hold your tongue and just listen to the hopefully good story about why they are still at work. There better be a pregnant lady with a baby head stocking out.
You decide to let it slide because you have a hard time believing this person is capable of any kind of abuse, much less the variety she has described.
Inventory: Benefits of the Doubt: 16 left

* * *

I hope you're having fun at work.
Please call me.
We can do something together tonight.
YOU: The birthday boat already sailed, sorry! Maybe I'll bring ya back some leftovers.
HIM: Not even the same planet, and I'm sure I could find a different planet. I'd rather eat at home than in a restaurant.
YOU: What if you want to go to a restaurant on a different planet?

HIM: That sounds like something that would happen.
YOU: Why did you say that?
HIM: Because it sounded interesting.
YOU: Are you saying I'm boring?

HIM: I am not bored. I'm tired.
YOU: What happened to the birthday party?
HIM: It didn't work out.
YOU: What happened?
Did the party get tired of you?

HIM: No, they had too many other things to do.
YOU: I see. So, how are you feeling today?
HIM: Good.
YOU: That bad, huh?

HIM: It was just a little bit awkward.
YOU: Awkward, hmm...
HIM: I know.
YOU: Do you need to talk about it?
Or I can get you a dream journal if its too embarrassing.

HIM: I don't mind talking about it.
YOU: Okay then. I know how that goes.

HIM: How what goes?
YOU: Talking about stuff.
HIM: Oh, yeah.
YOU: Well, I know how it feels when someone talks about their problems.
If you hear me make jerk-off sounds you just me to ask to stop and then I'll think about it.

HIM: I guess that makes sense. I don't know why I said anything, though.
YOU: I have no idea either.
HIM: You're right.
YOU: Damn right.

HIM: I know it's been hard for you.
YOU: It has.
HIM: I'm sorry.
YOU: Me too.

dataFragment.data: [What is the deal with the difficulty levels? Tell me a bit about the logic.]

Well the game has five settings for difficulty and they are designed so that people can play them from start to finish. Each setting has its challenges tailored for people at different skill levels, so if you find you've hit a level where you are just unable to beat it and you've lost hours on it (as opposed to losing to it once and saying screw it), then switch up the next time.

It started as something we thought would make the game more fun. The main difference was that we could use a higher power, and it would do whatever they wanted instead of whatever I did. So there's more variety in gameplay because we didn't get a say over how much we'd get to affect things.

For example, I could use a curse word to lower their character stat. A normal guy might do this and go to hell. But my husband couldn't curse because I made it a rule, and the game kept saying I was using an inane amount of luck to do it, but we were just playing by a different set of rules, not really trying hard enough, etc...

Then we added the god part. Now he has free will, but it can only be used for good (in moderation) because we had him swear oaths and promises about what his choices were doing. It made sense at first, until I found a bug that meant if we took it far, it would become too random. So the last level we released is basically "you win the lottery," but you have no money or anything and everyone hates you. The end.

[The game has created a new spectrum for us to debate over, one brought about by the games rabid followers, so rabid that it seems an inverse gamergate is on the horizon. Tell us about the Toxic/Caustic spectrum. What is the difference and how does the game apply this concept?]

Toxic - In my mind toxic describes people who are abusive. They are usually those in high places who think of themselves above all others. Caustic describes abusers whose actions seem cruel and unfair to the abuser.
We both fall into these categories. Abusers can sometimes come from seemingly innocent circumstances or positions of authority and power; and victims of abuse often get drawn into a position where they begin to think they deserve it, which creates the potential for the same kind of dynamic.

The abused snaps and then enacts the very rational response of beating someone’s ass. They have had it. No benefit of the doubt. Zero fucks. Grace says goodnight. I spit at you so I can pour this lye but im not gonna Tyler Duden ya to enlightenment. You know better, and now we are gonna see, after the lye is done dissolving, what’s left that’s worth keeping.”

The main cum rag responds to the abusive person saying, “Well you sure got some nice lumps on you now! I can barely feel them through all that dirt.”

Expectations and betrayal
In this situation, the expectations set forth for an interaction become the betrayal. The other becomes the abuser and you their victim. In the following, it’s easy to tell who’s doing it to whom.
You will know them by their utter lack of originality.

This isn’t just the repetition of an insult or the recycling of something said months ago, but when an abusive statement or action has been used on the protagonist many times in a single week with slight alterations, and nothing has changed, you’re in an environment that breeds abusive interactions with its own logic, rules, language. And this is how abuse thrives. By repetition of words, tones, gestures and behaviors which are so familiar and mundane they don’t require attention.
The audience the abuser cultivates get the illusion of a first time.

It is what it appears on the outside. It looks authentic and new. You’ve never heard the words before, you don’t recognize them and thus you have to process the whole scene, including their face, voice and mannerisms, for the first time and with great intensity—because everything is different.

Every word, every expression, the very air itself changes meaning, which makes the entire thing feel strange and surreal, even threatening. The words are not meant to be read. The only way to understand it is to experience it in a momentary flash as if it were the last thing your eyes would ever witness. It was like this: I can hear myself and my voice coming out, the sound waves vibrating the eardrums. That feeling was all.

And it embeds deeply into the memory of the abusers audience, they are given a context vastly different than the one the abused is groomed for. When the two contexts meet, what results is the abused seemingly defiling the most precious moment of the abuser’s cover story. Sometimes it is the ommission of one tiny detail, that changes the whole meaning of the story.

Other times the difference lies in how the event unfolds or ends and thus how the abuser wants it to end up. In both instances there exists only the potential of a scenario in which the abuser will have to endure another humiliating episode at the hands (or fists) of an innocent.

dataFragment.data: The simplest theory is always trviest, especially when you think about the human brain's propensity towards pattern matching and survival behaviors. Its why you see so many people with identical or near- identical traits that have no obvious connection at all and a huge number of personality disorders are actually commonalities amongst them. In psychology they say it like this. There is a difference, but not much between being depressed vs having OCD.

It may look superfically the same to a layperson or a therapist but in reality the differences can make a big differ ential impact.
I know you're confused, but here's the real kicker on how the mind of an abuser works and how it affects your interactions with them: The mind of an abuser functions like this in reverse, in terms of the brain's wiring.

They have this weird ability to filter and ignore any information that is inconsistent with their self- image, which makes it possible for them to be in relationships with total psychopaths and sociopaths. I don't care if your friend has blackouts or is an admitted alcoholic who beat you and threatened to burn your face, you know the way that person will treat everyone but you like trash because you know they would never do those things.

They wouldn't want to see someone else get treated badly or be made fun of and they would feel terrible if they were ever mean. It sounds crazy, right?! I promise you, if I'm sitting with two women friends at a party talking shop and my ex calls and we're in earshot I'll hang up on the phone and go off somewhere alone, no matter how much I hate it!

It's hard not to notice this kind of behavior because I'm not that dumb!
And I don't even mention abusive parents! The thing that gets most overlooked about emotional abusers is their absolute need for constant validation from people. Their idea of "control" is controlling other people, and if you give it enough attention they'll feel safe. I remember in high school this one guy had a lot of friends, lots of girls, a pretty decent social life... And that's about it.

Here are some warning signs. for those to whom these behaviors are new:

Sign #1 - The abuser starts by trying to dominate. For instance, if the woman wants the house to stay clean while the man works out of the bedroom, or is insisting he needs his own car to go into work on a daily basis. If this occurs with your friends and loved ones it's usually an indication the abuser will do similar in you and yours, and should serve as a clue you might need to start getting yourself away from this person.
Sign #2 -

Abusers have trouble admitting when they’re wrong. A simple apology won't cut it, nor can they apologize unless asked for something specific. This is one of many ways they're trying to exert control over you without ever being seen as wrong or needing correction, and that includes any behavior outside the relationship as well. When it becomes an issue with a close family member, this usually leads to denial about what they did wrong.
Sign #3 --

Abusive partners rarely leave things better than how you found them. If someone comes home from their partner after an evening of arguments and the house looks worse or they seem to be less presentable than usual, this could mean there's some damage left inside that they'd like repaired.
Sign #4 --

If the abusive partner seems angry all of the time (irritated/distracted/dismissive, hostile or aggressive), this might be due to the stress they feel being under your control has created for them as well. It also suggests a lot of time will have been spent justifying why you're in line with this abuser rather than with another, and the reason may lie somewhere inside yourself.
Sign #5 -- The lines between abuser and abuseee get fuzzzzzzzy.

The only way out may not be a divorce. It may just be leaving this place you live together in for more comfortable digs, moving into another home with a friend who will support your efforts at leaving. You need to find that line that will get the abuser the distance they want to maintain while making sure that they can't follow or come near you anymore.

Lies and gaslighting
Abuse involves repeated attempts to convince you your perceptions aren’t real. Gaslighting is a form that makes you doubt everything about your life and your perception. Lies are the other side of gaslighting, where abusers make it difficult to see what's right in front of them.

A good example of lies would be when you try to get someone who hates you to go out with you, only for them to flat-out lie about the date. In gaslighters mind, the date was a huge failure that never should’ve happened. It becomes impossible for them ever to agree to meet again after such dishonesty. The truth might actually cause them less distress because there’s less room to deny it, even if you were wrong.

This technique isn’t always malicious, however. Abusers may also believe what they're saying, and may genuinely not know how else to explain their situation, making it a reasonable choice for them. Regardless, you are still lied to. You could even argue the lie is a way to prevent any further harm to your relationship from an honest confrontation, so it’s abusive.

A common method for abusers in romantic relationships to gain more leverage in situations of disagreement and disagreement about their own treatment is to use a variation of gaslighting. For an abuser to be believed over someone else (particularly if said other person was a friend), they often begin lying, or simply exaggerating, events which led to their disagreement in order for the gaslit partner to look foolish in retrospect.

If their friends continue trying to reason with and confront them despite these obvious manipulations, it is an indication of deeper problems.

Her mother works in town so they rarely meet, but when they are close enough, her mother will hug her tightly before going off to wherever she goes and leaves the child with a stranger, who is her father's girlfriend.

Physical assault, sexual harassment
It would probably help to be told, explicitly and frequently, that they hate you. Abusers will also say hurtful things in front of others (usually family or friends), and even strangers sometimes, in order to demonstrate their control over you.
In addition, some of these techniques include actual physical harm: hitting you, punching you or otherwise hurting you physically, grabbing or pinching you painfully. Some of these acts are repeated over and over, making them more frightening and traumatic than the actual event, which makes them even more damaging than the threat. They also threaten and use weapons like guns or knives. The violence is meant to instill terror, fear, powerlessness and hopelessness.
This might seem obvious.

But if it wasn’t stated in the previous sections or shown through your abuser's actions and reactions, you could have trouble recognizing it. This is especially true for survivors of child sex abusers, who may find their abusers so frightening they don’t think about the abusive words or threats until years later when they encounter them again. It takes a lot of bravery to realize and confront these patterns. You have to understand your abuser and be able to look beyond all their nice smiles, charming behavior, charm and wit, and see how truly terrible this person is. If you can recognize that the words and actions of your abuser were designed to break you down—and you survived it and built yourself a stronger self—that's one hell of a good thing.

But to go that route requires great inner strength, courage and resolve, along with an awareness of your power to change your life, and your willingness to work towards a healthier relationship in spite of all the challenges ahead.

This section is a summary of a variety of different resources. Some were helpful for me, others didn’t quite work, but they’re listed here to be referenced in case someone else finds a link or resource that helps them out in similar ways. I'm hoping to provide this to a community wiki in the next week or so, to help us all remember our options. So if there's anything here you found helpful and/or you'd like to share it or contribute a page

or two to this section, let me know. You'll also find a handy guide to finding resources, including books to buy, on my web site (under the Resources tab) or in my book (in the Support & Community category), or on Amazon and Barnes & Noble.
There’s a lot of info in the resources I linked to, so it can be tough to wade your way through them all. But don’t worry, we have the same task ahead of us: we’re going to have to sift and cull the vast amount of data and misinformation out there to make it easier to know which resources are the most helpful to survivors, and the best to use with each particular person in need.

Here are some examples of misinformation about emotional abuse,  enjoy

1: There’s No Proof It Happens Because Emotion Isn’t A Factor in Science, and Science Has Found It to Not Be! Science doesn’t say what causes something; it says the best model available is this. In this model, everything from evolution to genetics to climate change and other natural phenomena influence all human actions, thoughts, beliefs, and interactions. Therefore emotions aren’t just irrelevant to these processes, but actively impede the understanding of the same. If you think emotions were important to scientific understanding, consider why the study that showed women who reported experiencing rape in childhood did so better at solving word problems was ignored. 2: Abusers Do This Only Because Women Lie About Being Assaulted. The statistics on sexual assault don’t lie.

And the numbers don’t lie when comparing men and woman. But there are many things about those statistics we simply don’t know because they don’t exist: e.g., the incidence rate, or number of abusers and victimization rates per year. Or maybe you want to talk percentages. How likely is your ex-husband to try something again? How much do the media influence public opinion and the legal system? 3: Abuse Is An Existential Horror Film. One of my favorite books about abuse and trauma was written for children, but it’s got so many useful bits to impart for adults too: For a while, you have no power, no voice, no one on your side. You don’t even see that there is anyone or a future to speak of—it’s like

being buried in the ground with only your arms above you. When someone hits you or shouts and screams at you and hurts you or tells you that you’re wrong or crazy or stupid—then it can feel a little less like it’s all happening to someone else. It can feel very real. And you don’t always get out of it by the skin of your teeth either. Sometimes it takes years. And there are times when the bad guys win, or if not the bad guy, a good guy you trusted. So what’s going to happen to you next time the abuser shows up at your door? What are you going to do about it this time and the hundredth or million and tenth? Are you prepared for the long road of therapy?

Abuse, it turns out is not a problem that exists in an environment separate from us. Abuse affects every single interaction with our families and friends. And every person that experiences the violence in any way is a survivor, even though each may be suffering through their experience differently than another. That doesn’t matter. You are also part of the solution, whatever the outcome of what happens in your personal life. 4: “You Have To Stop Saying All Men Will Be Abusers and Just Accept That People Get Mistreated Every Damn Day Of The Week” This statement is, unfortunately a common response to the question of why some people stay married to their abuser. This, by itself, indicates two things. Firstly it is evidence that the person asking the question doesn’t believe in abuse or isn’t listening at all,

because no intelligent person would be so blind.
But the bigger reason for the reaction to “stop saying all abusers are this and start recognizing that people get mistreated” is an attempt to invalidate the victim’s experience by minimizing the pain they went through or ignoring their right to speak up about what happened to them, despite a lack of willingness to understand. There are plenty of cases in the world where abuse has taken place, but where there was never the chance to leave, nor the resources to seek support outside. And that, ladies, is exactly the issue with these kinds of statements. No one knows for sure what makes a marriage survive and what will ultimately break one. There have been studies which indicate women who are sexually assaulted are four times as likely to divorce their partner than non-victims (source, wikipedia).

In other words, sexual violence increases the risk of ending the union, not only the abuse itself, but it changes the odds in favor of breaking it up, making a marriage more prone to the risks involved. So saying all abusers aren’t abusive isn’t an attempt to justify abuse, its a way of attempting to lessen it, or, as I’ve stated earlier to blame and discredit the victim’s experience. If we stop thinking of abusers only in abstract terms, where they don’t affect anyone around us and can only ever take place inside a specific relationship and then, when it’s a friend of ours who is being abusive and controlling instead of a total stranger. The chances increase that those victims will have access to support and, if it doesn’t work the first time, will learn

the skills to help them find alternative ways out without leaving their partners behind them.
It should go without stating that the fact the abuser’s a member of our society or that it’s someone we’re very close to doesn’t change anything. Abuse can be directed toward children, a family member or even someone who has been a teacher or therapist of yours. What matters, in all these situations, is how they interact with the rest of their surroundings and how that impacts them, not how many degrees of separation you or I are from the abuse. But, what about the perpetrator’s actions? They are also members of our society, which gives rise to questions such as, how is this person not being stopped before he hurts so many more of our brothers and sisters.

Why hasn’t he been jailed yet?
To answer that: because his victims, the real ones and the false ones alike, have never felt safe to talk. The police might think it's a domestic dispute or they would look the other way. In cases where there are children in danger, there is always the chance they will be labeled as liars and told that what happened was a game of pretend and nothing serious happened.
This brings me to my next point: abusers can come in many shapes and forms.
In this particular simulator, a lot has to do with the environment and culture in which the abuse took place, or is happening now. For instance: a woman whose spouse hits her in public could have done the same thing at home but it’s less risky to hit a passerby.

She can't hit back, but if she tells her friends what happens to her in public then she might feel safe to say that about her husband at home too. This is an extreme, of course; you don’t hear many women complaining that the men they date have to hit them because they are so much better than us. It takes courage and confidence to speak out and that's something most abused women can agree is in scarce supply. And I say it’s rare because we still hear stories from survivors of the war-like days. When people didn’t speak out about abuse, those of their friends who dared to did so and suffered retaliation, including murder, which meant no one dared. There were other things to fear as well, like going through life with a mark that might follow them.

A man can beat his wife and get away with it. A girl who complains gets punished, but if she's lucky enough to get married again then her husband won’t kill her, he'll give the other guy the same treatment. In a way this is good news for women, though I think most girls are aware that the odds aren’t so great. The odds don’t matter when the alternative means death. So, even with all the good in our history we are nowhere near perfect yet, and we haven’t changed anything since our ancestors fought the battle for survival in a very dangerous world. It doesn’t take much for a person to believe their life depends on them, and so they don’t try and make any noise.

That’s why we don’t hear about more abuse until someone does stand up and makes themselves known and then that might be after the abuser beats them and kills the child. If you've ever heard about the beating that leads to murder, it might have sounded as if no one had a clue. You can tell it to be sure.
Now you see the importance of knowing the difference between a game of hide and seek and being the prey, or at least pretending that. I know how difficult it must be to live in a constant state of vigilance but if we do not learn from these mistakes and move toward a solution that is more like what I’ve been trying to convey with this essay than just another article about domestic abuse then how much more will we suffer?

You have to wonder if the only hope we have for stopping these horrors are in the hands of the abusers themselves, because otherwise the problem isn’t solvable in time. I'm glad that you have come to my aid, I am. I would have fallen off this horse and out of sight a long while ago if you weren’t, and thank you, I do mean it from the bottom of my heart. It’s nice to know that somebody cares. And you, you do seem to. Thank you, again, and sorry to say it’s not enough.

If so then why is this a woman thing in the first place? What you call "game" seems different from what the majority of us are familiar with (in which the goal is escape) -- although admittedly there are plenty of similarities to the kinds of activities you describe here and how people tend to play games online... and I can understand why people think of it like that, it sounds quite a bit like a game in a number of ways, though it also seems to differ in important respects too, in fact some things that sound quite like games (and which may be called by other names) turn out to not really resemble the sorts of social activities we know and are comfortable with... but the point is that this sort of activity and many other online communities exist for the sake of pleasure, or at least the illusion of it, which may explain the

similarity to what most people consider gaming... but anyway you can probably find people playing it who would just say "it doesn't seem much like a 'gamer' game," if anything, it seems like more of a "game for masochists and other freaks," at any rate, whether the term fits depends on one's definition of what constitutes the typical "gamming lifestyle"
And that leads me to believe that perhaps the "masochism thing" has nothing at all to do with it. It may simply not be the sort of social interaction that's usually understood as part of what it means to be human in the first place. The people who engage in it have found that they enjoy the results. It seems to fulfill a need that's separate from the "social game" and so, rather than "playing a role" that we

understand the way the average person understands it (e.g., pretending to be a nice guy when you want something), they instead adopt an alter-ego, or persona, of some sort, who serves no functional purpose. I've heard of several people with severe Asperger syndrome and autistic tendencies engaging in this activity, including some people on SA, but the ones I personally met all seemed to fall into the category I mentioned, with some people having interests beyond "just game," as in their work. And while the whole situation seems to have arisen because they needed some sort of outlet, that may be a misleading characterization, given that there may be an underlying drive behind the phenomenon. But regardless of the origin of it all, once they discovered that it had certain satisfying elements to it, these "freaks," who'd probably not even self

-identify as "players," became regulars. They've created a niche that exists for their pleasure and the benefit of those that wish to emulate them and/or seek out new experiences, and that they themselves might have enjoyed at a younger age, and so are able to relate to, but they don't really identify as "gaming players," which to my mind seems like the wrong term to use, especially since they wouldn't normally be thought of in that manner... and the way they refer to it makes it clear that the terms overlap somewhat, and the people who engage in it may have very little understanding or interest at all about "game culture," except for how the activity serves their personal satisfaction. I know, the last paragraph was a real mouthful...

let me try to explain what I'm saying with more detail in subsequent messages and comments.
There were many others that came to mind in reading through SA, but that one in particular stuck out to me as being of particular note. While I can see the appeal of "gamesmanship," as described by another player, I think there's another level that they're describing: playing roles.
If you read the entire message again with the idea of playing roles in mind and how some folks are able to take the same action without feeling any of the associated discomfort, you might realize that they are not really talking about a masochistic desire. Rather, this seems like they're speaking of an opportunity to experience the same sense of power they find from interacting with an NPC.

The sense of empowerment is in turn, perhaps a subtext to why this sort of gaming occurs, but that isn't my focus at present.
My goal in the future may or may not involve creating and writing about games. If I did write a book, the focus would certainly center around what happens during play. But even if a project like this never materializes, I still have other reasons for continuing with the SA.

So now, what's my plan going forward? What can I do right away to contribute to making SA a better, more interesting place? Here are a few thoughts, though they could use a good amount of fine-tuning.
--
First and foremost: continue working on my contributions. It is, as I said earlier, the only thing of value to my life.

I am not going to let that slip through my fingers, especially since it will take me out of contact with all of you wonderful, kind folks. I will be contributing the way that has always proven to be effective: by making things.
I have several different projects that I've worked on, but that one I started recently, a web app called Moot, was designed to be an easier and simpler solution to the common task of gathering notes and ideas. So, now, instead of taking notes and saving text in separate apps and folders (because those are tedious and slow to work with and you can end up losing them) I just save them into one folder inside of the browser. The folder can hold images and other content and be shared among all of your various computers.

I'm in no position to create an open platform like this myself, but someone else who does could make something great.
But I want my own site for Moot to eventually become a website. For the time being, I don't have enough content to support that and it would just get buried under the endless stream of new posts from all of you, so that will be put on hold until I finish my other work. I think this means the next version of Moot will include a forum. It's been a while since there's an active online community on SA. The only exception is our local LARP community which meets regularly, but there is very little communication outside of their regular meetings.
In fact, the whole purpose behind creating Moot was so that I had something I can use to start a thread here and see what happens when

I say, hey look, there is something I think would be useful and maybe some folks would find it entertaining. If that happens, then the site becomes the main reason I continue writing about the topic of Emotional Abuse, not because of the blog, or a particular book. In my mind, Moot was a sort of trial run. I want a community on this board, a safe haven for discussion, so that if it fails miserably and the community dissolves, the SA community won't be devastated. And, to answer some of your comments in a previous blog post about my own writing process: I have written a ton. Not everything gets posted on SA. But every time a piece goes on the blog, it gets put up at least twice before.

It might be that this story gets turned in to fiction or that it turns out to be more compelling than expected.
But this time around, I wanted to give my stories to an editor to read. I thought the editors on the SA community could help with the editing, too, and they were able to suggest things to fix and make me better with that kind of feedback. This was the most successful experience I'd ever had and so, after talking with the admins and some other writers about how the idea for the community came to pass, it seemed reasonable to try it again, on a larger scale. And the result was Moot, and it looks to have been quite popular.
But I'm not happy with how much work it takes to manage.

There has to be a solution, and soon, or this whole thing falls apart and everyone gets frustrated and moves on. But that means we've got to come up with a way of running the board where people are happier than the last one was. Maybe that's asking for too big a task, especially given how much we have to get done right now (and, you know, there are a lot of other problems with the site).
I don't expect this post will be very helpful to anyone in solving those problems. So let me say instead that this project is worth trying to keep on the rails, and maybe some people reading it might feel a twinge of guilt or self-hatred and think to stop, take a breath, reevaluate what they're doing, maybe see if there are other ways to deal.

It also feels worthwhile to say: This happened to me and the first draft took four weeks, the edit and proofreading was a month, I went through another two months on revision before going out to beta testers, the website design came together pretty quickly but cost us over a hundred bucks. I didn't write anything about my personal or intimate experience, so if this helps you, you are welcome.

There is a certain degree of anger in every emotion. Emotions that do have an angry component to them will tend to focus it. The angry feeling of betrayal will, when it becomes rage and you throw a fist at someone you love and they duck, hurt more than if you’d never felt it in the first place.

When the anger fades, the person you punched feels a little empty and lost, and the wound it caused hurts worse for it. That pain lingers for days after.
This isn’t just about violence either. Anger can make people mean. They might not be violent physically, but they are verbally and sometimes psychologically abusive to their partners, children, or friends. People become afraid of the fury that erupts within, which they think is just their anger at something someone else did, or fear for the safety and welfare of themselves and their relationships with the other people in question, but in truth they are only reacting in anger. Their feelings of sadness are just masking anger; they are, like most abusers, acting on their emotions.

This kind of abuse is often referred to as silent rage or passive-aggressive violence, since it happens behind closed doors.
Abusers may use this type of behavior to keep the victim dependent upon them or to exert control over the other people in a particular group. In any relationship, one of you may be prone to using it and one not. It doesn’t make one better or worse than the other. If you’re having trouble identifying whether your own partner might be guilty, then read about the traits listed above to find the answer.
Emotional Abuse and Physical Violence
There are two types of emotional and psychological abuse: overt and covert.
Overt abuse has been clearly visible. There is no mistaking it when your spouse, lover, parent, or child tells you that you’re not good enough.

It might take the form of a physical assault, a threat, and verbal or written denigration of everything about your personality, body, and self-worth—and that's just what's obvious. Overt abuse takes different forms. You could say that there are many flavors of physical and sexual aggression. Some people don’t need to touch their partner in order to inflict harm. They just glare at him or her with a nasty look, a harsh tone, or the cold shoulders. Other times they punch or kick, and the blows are intended not only to cause pain but humiliation. Or, the person you care about might throw things, spit on you, or break or smash your belongings.

It is not possible to create an abuse simulator. There simply isn't enough material to work from; no single instance can be comprehensive enough. Instead, it was decided to have multiple scenes in order to give some variety and, hopefully, to provide a glimpse of what abuse actually looks like.

Each scene contains an abuser who appears for one segment. In most cases they appear at a moment where their abuse of the protagonist was especially bad, and the story proceeds as if they had appeared at any other point. For each scene they speak to the same characters as in Scene 1: mother and sister of the 11-year-old victim and the 10- and 8-year-old witnesses (in a manner which makes them complicitous with their abuser). Each segment has a separate plot line but the segments connect in ways that will be revealed throughout. In the end the perpetrator speaks only once, with each of three final segments containing him speaking at different moments, depending upon who survives.
Each scene ends by having each character leave the area in the same way.

If a person is abusive they may exit alone or leaving someone behind (usually with their back to the protagonist); however it should always seem as though the abuser exits without anyone accompanying them. If a nonabusive individual, be that mother, father, teacher or police officer or friend or acquaintance, is exiting, it is done by themselves, with nothing added, so that the abuse itself is made apparent through a contrast with an innocent or helpful party, rather than a happy ending. This is intended to simulate the idea that when a child tells a parent that something is happening, they will generally take it more seriously, while adults may ignore what a kid says. The same is applied for other parties, such as employers and colleagues. While it is acknowledged there may exist instances where abuse is covered up by those above a certain power, this particular simulators was

created to depict situations wherein such events were uncommon, even outside the home. The intention here, again, is to highlight how often an abused individual feels alone.
A couple points of emphasis: firstly, these simulations are designed to provoke feelings, not elicit them. It’s meant to bring about empathy and compassion rather than outrage. Empathy comes from feeling with another human, so the intent is that each person will identify strongly enough with their own self-perceived victims, or abusers, that this becomes obvious to them, and to some others. As the creator stated, this is all a bunch of bullshit but, as with everything else, it’s not meant as a commentary, and hopefully will instead be taken to mean “Hey!

Stop ignoring this stuff! I think your mom is abusing you, but if she were me, I’d never admit it because it hurts.”
The other key to remember is to try to keep in mind that abuse is rarely just about violence and physical attacks. There’s usually some form of emotional abuse, manipulation, or isolation included, too. This is meant to help remind us all that abuse isn’t solely about hitting, or threatening, or verbal harassment. All abuse is an attack against a victim’s self-esteem and, even with its less violent, but more insidious nature, is still deserving of compassion, not condemnation, as the goal is empathy and compassion. That’s why, while a lot of the scenarios will feel real and familiar to some people—because abuse has many faces,

including forms that can happen between spouses, parents and children or bosses and employees or teachers and pupils or coworkers or siblings or friends—each one is based on real experiences, and a specific example from someone’s own life who they can talk to. Each situation has the aim of illustrating, in detail, a particular form or manifestation of the most common type of emotional abuse, which is called the psychological, or psychodynamic form. The term, by definition, means an abuse that happens subconsciously, and often to those with low levels of intelligence, or those who lack a well-developed understanding or awareness of emotions, or even a vocabulary. The result of the psychological, or subliminal form of abuse, can manifest in different ways, including through subtle, indirect forms, or direct ones.

Some forms are subtle: a woman, after her husband, for example, accuses her of sleeping around and cheating. A more direct, and very visible one is to blame it on a man. When we think about it, both forms might look similar: they share the word abuse in them, and that, on the surface, seems like they’re describing the same thing. In fact, there are several differences. Firstly, with this kind of abuse, a relationship has already been formed. With a physical threat, no relationship exists. Another important distinction, which is related to that last, is the intention behind it. With a threat, the abuser wants you to submit to them and, therefore, a power hierarchy exists: you submit to him and you become lower than he, whereas when an accuser uses psychological abuse, no submission or relationship exists

. The abuser’s purpose is to make you lower, not themselves higher.
It doesn’t end here! Keep clicking on these images and you’ll find links that you may find useful to read about what the psychological, or “emotion-based,” variety of emotional abuse entails.

I want you to think of your own story and how it was affected.
What happened that made this person treat you like you’re a bad or lesser person? If they’re doing any of the tactics that I just outlined to manipulate and hurt others like you and me, then, yes. This is abuse. You have my full, unwavering support, whether you’ve experienced emotional, physical, sexual, or other types of abuse and how much.

If you haven’t suffered abuse in that way, or you were raised by a mother, father, brother, sister, grandmother, uncle, cousin, aunt, etc. and had a healthy upbringing that included a solid sense of self and the ability to express yourself without fear of judgment or rejection—or if you didn’t come from a situation with abusive adults, or none at all until you were 18 or older—it is possible you have never felt emotionally, physically, sexually or mentally abused by anyone, including your significant others. It’s even likely you don’t realize you have any issues around it, or what the effects could be, because it isn’t an area that gets talked about very much, and most people simply aren’t aware of its potential existence in the lives of the many

different genders. So let’s do our best to change that. Let’s start talking. We must make the issue and what’s behind the abuse, real for those who are affected. The first step is education. Please spread the word. Tell everyone, and more importantly listen to them. Share. Be open about your own feelings of abuse.
I hope I helped. Thanks for reading this far and sharing this with friends, or even better strangers. As we always say here, "You don't get to be human unless you learn empathy," and I know from the many letters I've received (which are archived) from those you care about that there is indeed plenty of empathy in all of us, and in the universe, so please share it.

Lies and gaslighting
Abuse involves repeated attempts to convince you your perceptions aren’t real. Gaslighting is a form that makes you doubt everything about your life and your perception. Lies are the other side of gaslighting, where abusers make it difficult to see what's right in front of them.

A good example of lies would be when you try to get someone who hates you to go out with you, only for them to flat-out lie about the date. In gaslighters mind, the date was a huge failure that never should’ve happened. It becomes impossible for them ever to agree to meet again after such dishonesty. The truth might actually cause them less distress because there’s less room to deny it, even if you were wrong.

This technique isn’t always malicious, however. Abusers may also believe what they're saying, and may genuinely not know how else to explain their situation, making it a reasonable choice for them. Regardless, you are still lied to. You could even argue the lie is a way to prevent any further harm to your relationship from an honest confrontation, so it’s abusive.

A common method for abusers in romantic relationships to gain more leverage in situations of disagreement and disagreement about their own treatment is to use a variation of gaslighting. For an abuser to be believed over someone else (particularly if said other person was a friend), they often begin lying, or simply exaggerating, events which led to their disagreement in order for the gaslit partner to look foolish in retrospect.

If their friends continue trying to reason with and confront them despite these obvious manipulations, it is an indication of deeper problems.

Physical assault, sexual harassment
It would probably help to be told, explicitly and frequently, that they hate you. Abusers will also say hurtful things in front of others (usually family or friends), and even strangers sometimes, in order to demonstrate their control over you.
In addition, some of these techniques include actual physical harm: hitting you, punching you or otherwise hurting you physically, grabbing or pinching you painfully. Some of these acts are repeated over and over, making them more frightening and traumatic than the actual event, which makes them even more damaging than the threat. They also threaten and use weapons like guns or knives. The violence is meant to instill terror, fear, powerlessness and hopelessness.
This might seem obvious.

But if it wasn’t stated in the previous sections or shown through your abuser's actions and reactions, you could have trouble recognizing it. This is especially true for survivors of child sex abusers, who may find their abusers so frightening they don’t think about the abusive words or threats until years later when they encounter them again. It takes a lot of bravery to realize and confront these patterns. You have to understand your abuser and be able to look beyond all their nice smiles, charming behavior, charm and wit, and see how truly terrible this person is. If you can recognize that the words and actions of your abuser were designed to break you down—and you survived it and built yourself a stronger self—that's one hell of a good thing.

But to go that route requires great inner strength, courage and resolve, along with an awareness of your power to change your life, and your willingness to work towards a healthier relationship in spite of all the challenges ahead.

Here are some examples of misinformation about emotional abuse,
enjoy

1: There’s No Proof It Happens Because Emotion Isn’t A Factor in Science, and Science Has Found It to Not Be! Science doesn’t say what causes something; it says the best model available is this. In this model, everything from evolution to genetics to climate change and other natural phenomena influence all human actions, thoughts, beliefs, and interactions. Therefore emotions aren’t just irrelevant to these processes, but actively impede the understanding of the same. If you think emotions were important to scientific understanding, consider why the study that showed women who reported experiencing rape in childhood did so better at solving word problems was ignored. 2: Abusers Do This Only Because Women Lie About Being Assaulted. The statistics on sexual assault don’t lie.

And the numbers don’t lie when comparing men and woman. But there are many things about those statistics we simply don’t know because they don’t exist: e.g., the incidence rate, or number of abusers and victimization rates per year. Or maybe you want to talk percentages. How likely is your ex-husband to try something again? How much do the media influence public opinion and the legal system? 3: Abuse Is An Existential Horror Film. One of my favorite books about abuse and trauma was written for children, but it’s got so many useful bits to impart for adults too: For a while, you have no power, no voice, no one on your side. You don’t even see that there is anyone or a future to speak of—it’s like

being buried in the ground with only your arms above you. When someone hits you or shouts and screams at you and hurts you or tells you that you’re wrong or crazy or stupid—then it can feel a little less like it’s all happening to someone else. It can feel very real. And you don’t always get out of it by the skin of your teeth either. Sometimes it takes years. And there are times when the bad guys win, or if not the bad guy, a good guy you trusted. So what’s going to happen to you next time the abuser shows up at your door? What are you going to do about it this time and the hundredth or million and tenth? Are you prepared for the long road of therapy?

Abuse, it turns out is not a problem that exists in an environment separate from us. Abuse affects every single interaction with our families and friends. And every person that experiences the violence in any way is a survivor, even though each may be suffering through their experience differently than another. That doesn’t matter. You are also part of the solution, whatever the outcome of what happens in your personal life. 4: “You Have To Stop Saying All Men Will Be Abusers and Just Accept That People Get Mistreated Every Damn Day Of The Week” This statement is, unfortunately a common response to the question of why some people stay married to their abuser. This, by itself, indicates two things. Firstly it is evidence that the person asking the question doesn’t believe in abuse or isn’t listening at all,

because no intelligent person would be so blind.
But the bigger reason for the reaction to “stop saying all abusers are this and start recognizing that people get mistreated” is an attempt to invalidate the victim’s experience by minimizing the pain they went through or ignoring their right to speak up about what happened to them, despite a lack of willingness to understand. There are plenty of cases in the world where abuse has taken place, but where there was never the chance to leave, nor the resources to seek support outside. And that, ladies, is exactly the issue with these kinds of statements. No one knows for sure what makes a marriage survive and what will ultimately break one. There have been studies which indicate women who are sexually assaulted are four times as likely to divorce their partner than non-victims (source, wikipedia).

In other words, sexual violence increases the risk of ending the union, not only the abuse itself, but it changes the odds in favor of breaking it up, making a marriage more prone to the risks involved. So saying all abusers aren’t abusive isn’t an attempt to justify abuse, its a way of attempting to lessen it, or, as I’ve stated earlier to blame and discredit the victim’s experience. If we stop thinking of abusers only in abstract terms, where they don’t affect anyone around us and can only ever take place inside a specific relationship and then, when it’s a friend of ours who is being abusive and controlling instead of a total stranger. The chances increase that those victims will have access to support and, if it doesn’t work the first time, will learn

the skills to help them find alternative ways out without leaving their partners behind them.
It should go without stating that the fact the abuser’s a member of our society or that it’s someone we’re very close to doesn’t change anything. Abuse can be directed toward children, a family member or even someone who has been a teacher or therapist of yours. What matters, in all these situations, is how they interact with the rest of their surroundings and how that impacts them, not how many degrees of separation you or I are from the abuse. But, what about the perpetrator’s actions? They are also members of our society, which gives rise to questions such as, how is this person not being stopped before he hurts so many more of our brothers and sisters.

Why hasn’t he been jailed yet?
To answer that: because his victims, the real ones and the false ones alike, have never felt safe to talk. The police might think it's a domestic dispute or they would look the other way. In cases where there are children in danger, there is always the chance they will be labeled as liars and told that what happened was a game of pretend and nothing serious happened.
This brings me to my next point: abusers can come in many shapes and forms.
In this particular simulator, a lot has to do with the environment and culture in which the abuse took place, or is happening now. For instance: a woman whose spouse hits her in public could have done the same thing at home but it’s less risky to hit a passerby.

She can't hit back, but if she tells her friends what happens to her in public then she might feel safe to say that about her husband at home too. This is an extreme, of course; you don’t hear many women complaining that the men they date have to hit them because they are so much better than us. It takes courage and confidence to speak out and that's something most abused women can agree is in scarce supply. And I say it’s rare because we still hear stories from survivors of the war-like days. When people didn’t speak out about abuse, those of their friends who dared to did so and suffered retaliation, including murder, which meant no one dared. There were other things to fear as well, like going through life with a mark that might follow them.

A man can beat his wife and get away with it. A girl who complains gets punished, but if she's lucky enough to get married again then her husband won’t kill her, he'll give the other guy the same treatment. In a way this is good news for women, though I think most girls are aware that the odds aren’t so great. The odds don’t matter when the alternative means death. So, even with all the good in our history we are nowhere near perfect yet, and we haven’t changed anything since our ancestors fought the battle for survival in a very dangerous world. It doesn’t take much for a person to believe their life depends on them, and so they don’t try and make any noise.

That’s why we don’t hear about more abuse until someone does stand up and makes themselves known and then that might be after the abuser beats them and kills the child. If you've ever heard about the beating that leads to murder, it might have sounded as if no one had a clue. You can tell it to be sure.
Now you see the importance of knowing the difference between a game of hide and seek and being the prey, or at least pretending that. I know how difficult it must be to live in a constant state of vigilance but if we do not learn from these mistakes and move toward a solution that is more like what I’ve been trying to convey with this essay than just another article about domestic abuse then how much more will we suffer?

You have to wonder if the only hope we have for stopping these horrors are in the hands of the abusers themselves, because otherwise the problem isn’t solvable in time.
