So now, what's my plan going forward? What can I do right away to contribute to making SA a better, more interesting place? Here are a few thoughts, though they could use a good amount of fine-tuning.
--
First and foremost: continue working on my contributions. It is, as I said earlier, the only thing of value to my life.

I am not going to let that slip through my fingers, especially since it will take me out of contact with all of you wonderful, kind folks. I will be contributing the way that has always proven to be effective: by making things.
I have several different projects that I've worked on, but that one I started recently, a web app called Moot, was designed to be an easier and simpler solution to the common task of gathering notes and ideas. So, now, instead of taking notes and saving text in separate apps and folders (because those are tedious and slow to work with and you can end up losing them) I just save them into one folder inside of the browser. The folder can hold images and other content and be shared among all of your various computers.

I'm in no position to create an open platform like this myself, but someone else who does could make something great.
But I want my own site for Moot to eventually become a website. For the time being, I don't have enough content to support that and it would just get buried under the endless stream of new posts from all of you, so that will be put on hold until I finish my other work. I think this means the next version of Moot will include a forum. It's been a while since there's an active online community on SA. The only exception is our local LARP community which meets regularly, but there is very little communication outside of their regular meetings.
In fact, the whole purpose behind creating Moot was so that I had something I can use to start a thread here and see what happens when

I say, hey look, there is something I think would be useful and maybe some folks would find it entertaining. If that happens, then the site becomes the main reason I continue writing about the topic of Emotional Abuse, not because of the blog, or a particular book. In my mind, Moot was a sort of trial run. I want a community on this board, a safe haven for discussion, so that if it fails miserably and the community dissolves, the SA community won't be devastated. And, to answer some of your comments in a previous blog post about my own writing process: I have written a ton. Not everything gets posted on SA. But every time a piece goes on the blog, it gets put up at least twice before.

It might be that this story gets turned in to fiction or that it turns out to be more compelling than expected.
But this time around, I wanted to give my stories to an editor to read. I thought the editors on the SA community could help with the editing, too, and they were able to suggest things to fix and make me better with that kind of feedback. This was the most successful experience I'd ever had and so, after talking with the admins and some other writers about how the idea for the community came to pass, it seemed reasonable to try it again, on a larger scale. And the result was Moot, and it looks to have been quite popular.
But I'm not happy with how much work it takes to manage.

There has to be a solution, and soon, or this whole thing falls apart and everyone gets frustrated and moves on. But that means we've got to come up with a way of running the board where people are happier than the last one was. Maybe that's asking for too big a task, especially given how much we have to get done right now (and, you know, there are a lot of other problems with the site).
I don't expect this post will be very helpful to anyone in solving those problems. So let me say instead that this project is worth trying to keep on the rails, and maybe some people reading it might feel a twinge of guilt or self-hatred and think to stop, take a breath, reevaluate what they're doing, maybe see if there are other ways to deal.

It also feels worthwhile to say: This happened to me and the first draft took four weeks, the edit and proofreading was a month, I went through another two months on revision before going out to beta testers, the website design came together pretty quickly but cost us over a hundred bucks. I didn't write anything about my personal or intimate experience, so if this helps you, you are welcome.

Emotionless
There is a certain degree of anger in every emotion. Emotions that do have an angry component to them will tend to focus it. The angry feeling of betrayal will, when it becomes rage and you throw a fist at someone you love and they duck, hurt more than if you’d never felt it in the first place.

When the anger fades, the person you punched feels a little empty and lost, and the wound it caused hurts worse for it. That pain lingers for days after.
This isn’t just about violence either. Anger can make people mean. They might not be violent physically, but they are verbally and sometimes psychologically abusive to their partners, children, or friends. People become afraid of the fury that erupts within, which they think is just their anger at something someone else did, or fear for the safety and welfare of themselves and their relationships with the other people in question, but in truth they are only reacting in anger. Their feelings of sadness are just masking anger; they are, like most abusers, acting on their emotions.

This kind of abuse is often referred to as silent rage or passive-aggressive violence, since it happens behind closed doors.
Abusers may use this type of behavior to keep the victim dependent upon them or to exert control over the other people in a particular group. In any relationship, one of you may be prone to using it and one not. It doesn’t make one better or worse than the other. If you’re having trouble identifying whether your own partner might be guilty, then read about the traits listed above to find the answer.
Emotional Abuse and Physical Violence
There are two types of emotional and psychological abuse: overt and covert.
Overt abuse has been clearly visible. There is no mistaking it when your spouse, lover, parent, or child tells you that you’re not good enough.

It might take the form of a physical assault, a threat, and verbal or written denigration of everything about your personality, body, and self-worth—and that's just what's obvious. Overt abuse takes different forms. You could say that there are many flavors of physical and sexual aggression. Some people don’t need to touch their partner in order to inflict harm. They just glare at him or her with a nasty look, a harsh tone, or the cold shoulders. Other times they punch or kick, and the blows are intended not only to cause pain but humiliation. Or, the person you care about might throw things, spit on you, or break or smash your belongings.

It is not possible to create an abuse simulator. There simply isn't enough material to work from; no single instance can be comprehensive enough. Instead, it was decided to have multiple scenes in order to give some variety and, hopefully, to provide a glimpse of what abuse actually looks like.

Each scene contains an abuser who appears for one segment. In most cases they appear at a moment where their abuse of the protagonist was especially bad, and the story proceeds as if they had appeared at any other point. For each scene they speak to the same characters as in Scene 1: mother and sister of the 11-year-old victim and the 10- and 8-year-old witnesses (in a manner which makes them complicitous with their abuser). Each segment has a separate plot line but the segments connect in ways that will be revealed throughout. In the end the perpetrator speaks only once, with each of three final segments containing him speaking at different moments, depending upon who survives.
Each scene ends by having each character leave the area in the same way.

If a person is abusive they may exit alone or leaving someone behind (usually with their back to the protagonist); however it should always seem as though the abuser exits without anyone accompanying them. If a nonabusive individual, be that mother, father, teacher or police officer or friend or acquaintance, is exiting, it is done by themselves, with nothing added, so that the abuse itself is made apparent through a contrast with an innocent or helpful party, rather than a happy ending. This is intended to simulate the idea that when a child tells a parent that something is happening, they will generally take it more seriously, while adults may ignore what a kid says. The same is applied for other parties, such as employers and colleagues. While it is acknowledged there may exist instances where abuse is covered up by those above a certain power, this particular simulators was

created to depict situations wherein such events were uncommon, even outside the home. The intention here, again, is to highlight how often an abused individual feels alone.
A couple points of emphasis: firstly, these simulations are designed to provoke feelings, not elicit them. It’s meant to bring about empathy and compassion rather than outrage. Empathy comes from feeling with another human, so the intent is that each person will identify strongly enough with their own self-perceived victims, or abusers, that this becomes obvious to them, and to some others. As the creator stated, this is all a bunch of bullshit but, as with everything else, it’s not meant as a commentary, and hopefully will instead be taken to mean “Hey!

Stop ignoring this stuff! I think your mom is abusing you, but if she were me, I’d never admit it because it hurts.”
The other key to remember is to try to keep in mind that abuse is rarely just about violence and physical attacks. There’s usually some form of emotional abuse, manipulation, or isolation included, too. This is meant to help remind us all that abuse isn’t solely about hitting, or threatening, or verbal harassment. All abuse is an attack against a victim’s self-esteem and, even with its less violent, but more insidious nature, is still deserving of compassion, not condemnation, as the goal is empathy and compassion. That’s why, while a lot of the scenarios will feel real and familiar to some people—because abuse has many faces,

including forms that can happen between spouses, parents and children or bosses and employees or teachers and pupils or coworkers or siblings or friends—each one is based on real experiences, and a specific example from someone’s own life who they can talk to. Each situation has the aim of illustrating, in detail, a particular form or manifestation of the most common type of emotional abuse, which is called the psychological, or psychodynamic form. The term, by definition, means an abuse that happens subconsciously, and often to those with low levels of intelligence, or those who lack a well-developed understanding or awareness of emotions, or even a vocabulary. The result of the psychological, or subliminal form of abuse, can manifest in different ways, including through subtle, indirect forms, or direct ones.

Some forms are subtle: a woman, after her husband, for example, accuses her of sleeping around and cheating. A more direct, and very visible one is to blame it on a man. When we think about it, both forms might look similar: they share the word abuse in them, and that, on the surface, seems like they’re describing the same thing. In fact, there are several differences. Firstly, with this kind of abuse, a relationship has already been formed. With a physical threat, no relationship exists. Another important distinction, which is related to that last, is the intention behind it. With a threat, the abuser wants you to submit to them and, therefore, a power hierarchy exists: you submit to him and you become lower than he, whereas when an accuser uses psychological abuse, no submission or relationship exists

. The abuser’s purpose is to make you lower, not themselves higher.
It doesn’t end here! Keep clicking on these images and you’ll find links that you may find useful to read about what the psychological, or “emotion-based,” variety of emotional abuse entails.

Her brother came out, told everyone the details about what a shit the dad had been, but how it wasn't until the last two years that she felt like something had to change in their relationship, so she's finally telling the story of her abuse. Everyone laughs nervously, and after a few drinks her brother tells him that the story about him getting into a fight is bullshit and he didn't punch the kid in the nose. But then it was true. And they were just joking, and he didn't remember, it had happened so long ago, and now she doesn't either and this whole conversation was ridiculous, and she didn't think the mom even knew the dad had done that and what the kid thought was a punch was
Looking from a far, the boyfriend (is that what I am?)  is seeing gas pumped in from four different utility companies, three of which say they are pumping solar power.

In one scene the sun shines bright off an open field and a farmer working a combine sees that and shouts "That can’t be, there is a hole through your roof," which is clearly meant to evoke memories of someone's father pointing out that there's no money for repairs and you have to put up with whatever damage happens. The final company pumps in coal and is obviously a villain who needs punishment, the sort of punishment where they don't get paid, their children have to work to keep things running, and it's all a lie, but the real thing will be worse and it might never end if you can't get this solved. They are also being watched by a government employee who is recording what's happening. They've already met her and it's clear that her main purpose for being there has to do with getting a look at
the firm butts of all the men of the family, it was later found. She had no business being there at all.
Not even American, can you believe that?

--
Taunting and intimidation
They know that you're weak, and use fear, anger, and anxiety to manipulate and control you, making you want to give up on your life.
You might feel a desire for violence, even though the odds are very low you'll ever actually commit an act, or a wish to stop speaking. They take advantage of that feeling and tell you you should kill yourself so you won't embarrass them anymore, which they say over and over until their threats are all you can think about.
They play on your feelings, so you want to believe that everything will go your way; when you do, you find it easier to let yourself fall. When your fears are high, it's easier to lose your grip.
Nah brah, you make like you are breaking down. Go the ol' Hamlet. Let them believe yer bonkers. They will let THEIR guards down. Then you can land the blows you need.

--
Shaming
Abuse is not all about hitting. They use shame and criticism to make you doubt who you really are and what you’re doing with your life. The following are just some ways they make you doubt yourself:
Calling you ugly or worthless or dumb
Being condescending to you (“You’re a big boy. Why can’t you do this?” “It would help me out a lot if YOU could help ME with THIS!” “Do as you are TOLD.”)
Criticizing your taste in food, clothes, or music or anything else.
Demanding perfection, like “you’re supposed to get this right the first time.

” This is especially common if you don’t have the tools you’re supposed to need, such as the ability to type and the skill of grammar and syntax.
Asking you questions like, “Have you tried to kill yourself yet?,” or telling you how it must be so painful for your mother because her father did something like that. Or telling her father stories about her father’s mistakes, just to drive her point home. They use these to make you look weak. They want you to feel small and unworthy, but it’s important to keep your eyes on their hands. If you focus only on their face, it becomes a blank expression, masking the true intentions behind their words.

Welcome to the Emotional Abuse Simulator 6.0, please submit your request for certificate at the end of the session.
And please memorize the safe-gesture that will be your personalized cue to end the program. Excellent, let's begin stepping through the doorway.
***
You are a human, and your identifiers are inconsequential and can oscillate within the narrative if you want.
It's your birthday! Your partner has a big surprise for you when they come home from work! They know how special this day is for you. After much challenge to get past your hang-ups and actually ask for what you want, you say, "I just want a simple night at home, maybe some wine, but totally not a requirement."
Your partner asked if you wanted food from this restaurant or that one. You took your pick, and have been waiting to get a link from him. Not wanting to seem a nag you give them two potential orders depending on what they decide. Not wanting to disrupt their workflow. You think nothing of it until the end of your workday.
The commute home, you started to feel a tiny twinge of anxiety. You have two possible dinners before you. Not knowing which is the yeast upon which the bread of your anxiety rises. The writing team in your head says cringe at the lame metaphor and they say ya can't win them all.
Your cat mewls, you already fed it. What? Mewl. Whatcha need? Mewl. Christ! You try to ignore the cat.
After getting home and taking a shower, your hands start shaking. You lay down, you hate this part of yourself that wants clear directions or have a 10 minute breakdown when those plans change. You try to calm yourself. You put on some TV to clear the chattering in your head, which whittles down to one audio track outside your head and allowing you to float calmly.
Your breathing slows, while on the TV, the news cycles through a new story on gender and privilege in America.
What you really needed was to hear someone else say you're right about this without anyone ever leaving with your secret.
At this moment, in the middle of the evening news, you feel it. There are moments when everything comes together, the timing perfect, a piece falls into place.
It seems absurd.
You've spent so much time trying to make sense of the world. But you feel like it could work. You feel a smile on your face, and you realize you haven't smiled in years.

You turn off the TV and get ready to go out.
"What are you doing?" asks your partner.
"Going to eat out."
"That's what you said earlier!"

"Well, we changed our minds."
"I can see that. I don't want to leave my job early. I have work to do!"
You sit down, and your partner starts to cook.

You watch them move around the kitchen and notice that they're wearing a short skirt and heels. You start to feel uncomfortable and begin to fidget with your phone.
Your partner notices this and walks over.
"Are you okay?" she asks.
"Oh, sorry! Yes, yes, I'm fine!"
She puts her arms around you and holds you tight. She strokes your hair and kisses your cheek.
"You smell nice," you say.
"Why thank you! Do you want a glass of wine? Or maybe some tea?"

"Maybe a little bit of both, actually," you say.
A few hours later, you come home and find your partner still there. You walk through the door and she sees you and smiles.
"Hi love!"
"Hey honey, how was work?"
"Ugh, you know. Boring shit."
You give her a kiss.
"Want a cup of coffee?"
"Love to," you say.
The next morning, you wake up in bed. Your partner's arm is draped across you, and she's lying on her side facing you.

Her eyes are closed, and her breath is slow and steady.
You lie awake for a long time. The sun has risen, and it's shining brightly through the window. The birds are singing. There's a slight chill in the air, but otherwise it looks like any other spring day.
You open your mouth to say something, but you don't know what it should be. You think of your life. You wonder how it got this way. What happened between last night and today that put you here? Why didn't you leave sooner?
But then you remember your partner's warm body beside you, and you relax.

He must have known you wouldn't go. So you roll over and sleep in his embrace.
At one point, he stirs and moves away from you. His breathing gets deeper, and after a few minutes, you hear him snoring quietly.
He wakes up soon after, stretches, and leans on his elbow. Then he rolls onto his side facing you.
"Good morning," he says.
You reach out and touch his hand. It feels cold.
"Morning," you say.
"Are you okay?" he asks.

"Yes. Sorry, I guess I fell asleep. I can't believe you stayed here."
"I'm glad you did."
"Me too," you say.
You lean into him.
***
When you were first born, you had a condition called hydrocephalus. It left you with a large, fluid-filled head. Doctors operated on you, shaving away part of your skull and inserting a shunt to drain your brain.
As a result, you grew up feeling different than everyone else. You struggled to understand things that other kids picked up on easily.

You never felt truly safe or comfortable, because you couldn't hide the fact that you weren't quite right.
One day, you went to school with your parents. Everyone stared at you. The principal tried to explain why, but you didn't really care. That was when you started to realize that you were going to be ostracized forever.
That year, you stopped trying to fit in. Instead, you hid in the corner and read books until it was time for you to go home. Eventually, your mother moved you to a private school for children like yourself.

There, you learned to be who you needed to be, instead of who anyone wanted you to be. It's hard to describe the relief you felt. Being around others with the same problems—whether mental or physical—felt comforting. At least now you knew you weren't alone.
But it wasn't enough to just cope with your issues. Soon, you realized that the most difficult part of having a disability is knowing there's a world out there that doesn't expect anything from you. That's when your anxiety began to increase.
Your new classmates and teachers seemed happy with their lives, but you always felt like an outsider looking in.

Maybe that's why you spent so much time reading. In books, you could pretend you belonged somewhere.
By high school, you'd grown accustomed to being an outsider. You still had bad days, though. One particularly stressful week during your final semester, you barely spoke to anyone. You felt so lonely that you even considered transferring schools. But you loved your friends and teachers, and you didn't want to give up on them.
Then one night, your friend invited you to spend the weekend at his house. You weren't sure if it was a trick or not.

Then again, you thought maybe you should go. Who knows?
It turns out he wasn't lying. He gave you a tour of the place. Everything was neat and orderly. And, after the long week, you were exhausted. So you crawled into bed, eager to rest.
Once you lay down, your friend said, "We're going to play a game!"
"Okay," you said.
"Close your eyes, and then open them again when I tell you to," he told you.
So you closed your eyes.
"Open them," he said.

You opened your eyes.
"Now, can you see me?"
Yes, you saw him clearly.
He smiled.
"Good. Now, I'm going to count to three. When I say 'three,' you will wake up. Ready?"
Ready.
"One…two…three!"
And you woke up.
Your phone buzzed. It was your mother. You picked up.
"Hey Mom," you said. "I'm fine, I think."
She paused. She sounded worried.
"What's wrong?"

you asked.
"Oh, sorry baby. How did the party go last night? Are you okay?"
A chill ran through you.
"Mom," you said. "Is everyone really nice? Do I need to worry about anyone?"
Silence.
"I'm sorry, Mom. What did you say?"
"Are you okay honey? You sound strange. Is something wrong?"
You were quiet. You took a deep breath.
"Mom, please don't talk about this over the phone. We'll talk about it later."

You hung up.
You tried to go back to sleep, but your mind wouldn't shut off. You tossed and turned all night. Finally, you got up. You walked downstairs to the kitchen. You made yourself a cup of tea.
In the morning, you went to work. You sat quietly at your desk and worked until lunchtime. By then, your stomach was growling. You grabbed your jacket and headed home.
You opened the door.
"Hello dear," your mother called out.
You froze.
"Hi Mom," you replied.

She stepped forward.
"Would you like to come upstairs for some tea?"
"No thanks mom. I'm actually not feeling well. Maybe later."
"I brought you these cookies, dear," she said. "They're from my new recipe book. Would you like to try one?"
Your mouth felt dry.
"Sure," you managed.
She handed you a cookie. It tasted like ashes.
"Oh, thank you. That looks delicious. Can I have another one?"
Her smile grew wider.
"Of course," she said.

"You can eat two if you want. I don't mind."
"That sounds great."
"Here," she said, holding out a forkful of food.
"Thanks," you said.
You ate your cookie.
It was the best thing you'd ever eaten.
Your friend joined you for dinner. He complimented her cooking.
"Oh, you're very welcome," she said. "I'm glad you liked it."
Your friend had his own plate piled high with food.
"How long have you been living in Japan?"

he asked.
"Three years now," she said.
"It must be wonderful," he said. "So many beautiful places to visit, so much culture. Have you visited Kyoto yet?"
She smiled.
"Not yet," she said. "I've heard it's lovely there."
You looked at him.
"I thought you were going to write an essay on the Japanese legal system," you said. "You haven't started writing it yet, have you?"
He shook his head.
"It's a difficult topic," he said.

"And I'm having trouble deciding how to approach it."
"Well, have you written anything else?"
"Yes," he said. "I've been working on a few stories. A couple of short novels."
"What kind of stories? Are they fiction or nonfiction?"
"Both. It depends. My favorite is one of the nonfiction pieces I wrote last year. It's about a boy who has a rare disease that makes it impossible for him to cry. His parents are desperate to find a cure."
"Wow!" you said.

"That sounds pretty intense."
"Yeah, it is. But then I realized that most of us are probably experiencing similar situations on some level. We all experience loss and suffering—sometimes because of circumstances beyond our control. And we're afraid to let ourselves cry."
"Hmm. Yeah, that makes sense," you said.
"So I decided to write a story about someone who finds himself unable to cry after being abused. It's set in a post-apocalyptic dystopian society where everyone is required to wear masks to hide their real identities."

"Sounds interesting," you said.
"Yeah. It's coming along nicely. It'll probably be my first novel."
"Good luck with it," you said. "You seem to be handling your problems well, though. Not like me."
"Thanks. I appreciate that."
"No problem."
You finished your food. She took your dishes away.
"Thank you again for dinner," she said. "And thanks for letting me stay over."
"You're welcome. Glad you enjoyed yourself."
"I did."
"See you tomorrow," you said.

She nodded.
***
"How was work today?" you asked her.
"Good. It felt nice to finally put in some face time," she said.
"Was it weird seeing people after being gone so long?"
"A bit. But I had to admit, it actually helped a lot. I got to connect with a few friends from college. Worked on my resume a little. And met some new people too."
"Oh, cool! Did you talk about... stuff?"
"Yeah."
"Did you mention us?"

"Not at first, but toward the end they did ask."
"They didn't give you any shit, right?"
"No. They were very supportive."
"Well, good. I'm glad. So, um, can I come visit? Will you be around?"
"I'll be home during the week and we'll have a weekend together. You should definitely come down. I missed you so much."
"Me too. Can you send me some pictures?"
"Of course. I don't know when I'll be able to text them to you, but I'll send them soon."

"Okay, well, I better run. I hope you'll think of me when you're doing whatever you're doing. Just remember, I love you. You're amazing."
"I love you too, honey. Goodbye."
The woman hung up. You sighed, feeling relieved that you didn't have to break up with her. Then you remembered you'd never spoken to her before today. What had been going on in your relationship, exactly? Had you ever talked to each other before now? How far back did you need to go for there to be a baseline of trust between you?

What kind of horrible fuckery had you gotten into with this stranger?
You knew how to avoid such mistakes next time.
This isn't your fault. It's just the way it is.
So then why was it happening to you? Why you?
***
It feels like someone's watching me. I know I've seen that man somewhere before, but I can't place him. He keeps turning up, but he doesn't leave his car. Or maybe he just gets in and out of it.
I wonder if he's stalking me.

There must be cameras set up nearby. My heart pounds as I look over my shoulder. Is it because I'm paranoid? No. Because I've learned that I live in a surveillance state. The government collects data about me through every transaction, phone call, email, credit card purchase, social media update. They watch me while I sleep. They monitor my movements. They use facial recognition software to track me in public. They collect information about everyone I interact with. We are watched and followed everywhere we go.
He's still there. Still sitting behind the wheel, staring at me.

I start to walk faster. I don't know why I'm running away, but I can't bear to stay under those eyes anymore.
When I turn to look again, he's gone. I wait for several minutes, trying to catch sight of him, but he's nowhere in view. Maybe I imagined it. But what if I didn't? And if I did, then who is he? A friend? An enemy? Someone from work?
Why am I being followed?
I decide to drive around and find the location of the nearest camera.

I'll know once I've spotted it. If I spot it.
It's almost dark by the time I finally locate a cluster of CCTV cameras installed on light posts along the street. I pull off onto a side road. I get out of my car and stand near the sign. I can't see any cameras, but that doesn't mean there aren't any. I step back toward the curb and scan the area. I focus my gaze on one particular tree branch overhead, imagining that it's a security camera.
The branch seems to bob slightly, though I'm sure it's not moving at all.

I think I hear rustling leaves nearby. I imagine I see something move between two buildings, but when I turn to look directly, there's nothing there. I squint and listen hard. For a moment, I can hear someone whispering nearby, but it's impossible to determine whether or not it's coming from the street or the woods.
I'm starting to get cold, so I head back to my car and put the heater on high.
If I let myself panic, I won't be able to do anything.
I need to calm down and figure out what I'm dealing with.

What I know for certain is that someone is watching me. Not just anyone. Him. Who is he? Why was he following me?
I should call the police. I've seen enough movies and read enough thrillers to know that they're never friendly.
But what will I tell them? That I'm afraid someone's stalking me? How would that sound? Suspicious? Impossible? Paranoid?
No matter how I frame it, it sounds ridiculous. And no one needs to deal with my drama.
Besides, it could be a lot worse.

At least I haven't lost my job or my house yet.
I grab my phone and type an email to my therapist.
"Hi," I begin, "I'm writing you because I'm experiencing some serious stress right now. My boyfriend broke up with me a few weeks ago and since then, I've been getting followed everywhere I go. I don't know why, but I can't shake this feeling that he's watching me. I'm also concerned about losing my job. I applied for a new position over the weekend and was told I'd receive a reply within a week.

So far, I haven't heard anything. Also, I'm starting to suspect that some of the things happening in my personal life aren't accidental. I don't want to believe it, but I feel like I'm being manipulated somehow."

I'm not an expert on abuse.
This is a game, and I'm just writing about what I think abuse feels like.
There's been a lot of criticism over this simulator. I don't want to be part of the problem.
So let's talk about why there has been such a reaction to this simulation.
While I'm not an expert, I do consider myself an abuse afficianado.

For years I've been working with women who are victims of domestic violence.
When I first started doing this work, I was a lot younger, and a lot less knowledgable than I am today.
And there was one question that kept coming up again and again and again, time after time, from each woman I worked with:
"Why isn't anyone talking about me?"
Because you weren't talking about you, that's why.
Because no one asked.
No one heard you.
You didn't have a voice, because you never got to choose it.
And I keep forgetting to take pause and let you chime in, my bad.

I want to talk about your anger.
You're angry that someone stole something from you.
That they stole a part of yourself, and hid it away.
And for most of us, that's exactly what happened.
They stole something from you.
Something important. Something unique and valuable.
And they hid it in a box.
But then you grew up and the box disappeared. And now that's where the anger comes in.
It feels like they've taken the only thing you've ever had.
They took the only thing that was yours and made it theirs.
You ask the men in your town, "Where is my box?" And they snort, and they giggle, and you wonder what's so funny.

You try to figure out how the fuck your box got lost. You keep thinking that you'll find it.
But no one ever returns it.
No one has any answers for you, and no one ever talks about it.
You're angry and you're frustrated, but all you have is this empty box.
You spend the rest of your life trying to fill it. You want something to fill it, and you're tired of not being able to get what you want.
And that's why it feels so familiar.
And it sucks.
The head librarian gives a start and says, "Please say more about it, please?"

"It's an analogy. A simulation," I explain. "Like, there are all these things that happen in my life, and it's like they're happening to me in a movie. The emotions, the thoughts, everything. They're just..."
I make an exaggerated gesture of flipping through the air.
The head librarian stares at the screen and says, "A simulation?"
I nod. "Yes. Exactly."
She nods slowly. "So do you want me to talk you through it? Do you want me to make notes of all your responses?"
Head Librarian: All that and more.

I think it's time to talk.

I've never been one for long-term relationships. I can count the number of significant others and romantic partners I've had on the fingers of my hands. I like to be in and out—a quick, sharp cut that leaves me free to move on to something new and exciting before the scars have a chance to heal. But of all those short-term relationships, I've learned a few things. The biggest being that we're all just fucking garbage, and we will hurt each other.

It starts when we meet. In the first couple of dates, we want to be cool. We talk about sports, movies, and our jobs. The last thing we want to do is piss anyone off. When you have two people trying to make each other feel comfortable, you start to create little games. I like to start with the big picture—what do you want from this? What are your goals? Do you see marriage or children in the near future? As time goes on, these get smaller. Eventually they'll be something as simple as, "What do you do on your days off?"

or "Have you ever been on a real date?" You don't want to come off as a complete asshole, but it's important to find out where your boundaries are, and it's also important to test those boundaries. Sometimes people get angry. Other times they'll get silent, or cry. They might say nothing at all. Either way, you're getting closer.
Next comes the "I'm not looking for anything serious." This is a big one. It gives them room to back away without making the relationship awkward. If you hear this phrase in a bar or restaurant, there's no reason why you can't go home and hook up.

That way, they know you're open to seeing other people and won't be clingy. But if it's said after dinner at a nice restaurant, maybe a candlelit table overlooking the lake, then you're probably done. Because now, instead of thinking about your own needs, you have to think about theirs. What kind of future do they have? You'd be an asshole to suggest that someone would be happier single, so you keep quiet. Now you're alone with your thoughts—those dark ones. Do you just ignore their feelings or do you offer a hug?

Or a pat on the back? A quick, "Well, we can still be friends" leaves a lot more room to talk about the future. You can go home knowing that you did what was right. And they can go home too, knowing they didn't have to say it.
As the relationship moves into new territory, you start to realize how little you really know about your partner. You start to ask yourself: Do I trust this person? Am I in love with them? The longer you're with someone, the harder these questions become. Sometimes you don't know the answers, and sometimes you don't want to know the answer.
Sometimes you want to know the answer but not be obligated to show that you know the answer.

Because maybe you don't feel like you're ready to deal with all of this. Maybe you can't handle having to give answers to questions you don't understand, because you don't know how to answer them. Or maybe you just want to pretend that everything's okay, when you know it isn't. So you act as though you know the answer, and then you can move on.
Eventually, the questions are gone, but you're not happy. You don't have to ask them anymore, and yet you're still afraid of what you'll find out if you ask them again.

Maybe one day you're so unhappy you're ready to admit the truth. "I don't know how to feel," you say, or maybe you just don't say anything at all, but it comes out in other ways. And the worst part is, it's not the truth. You do know how to feel, but you don't like the truth, so you pretend you don't. You avoid your feelings.
But even avoiding them doesn't make them go away. They follow you around, until finally, you're too exhausted to hold onto them any more.

Fascinating article from Wired by Amanda Hess writing about 4chan & its founder Christopher Poole:
Chris started up the board not long after he bought his first home computer when he was fifteen years old, calling himself moot. He liked the anagram: a chatboard for discussion boards; Moot™, read aloud as two distinct words—like hearth and type —sounds nothing like moot itself, an experience far different from using Twitter, where most everyone uses one word for the whole thing and the tweeter usually keeps it short. Or rather, says Poole, they try.

Instead, when we use our phones, they amplify all these tics, bad puns, and teen-speak inclinations: "Texting makes you talk like text messages," he told me once. When he founded 4chan, it was this weird dynamic of rapid fire that became his hallmark.
Here's a little bit from his 'about' page there, if interested:
After graduating in 2010 with a BFA in Animation at NYU F.I.T., Chris began building sites with the skills he learned while working in ad agencies for five years prior. Through dabbling in user experience, interface design, interaction design and branding, he came to recognize his true passion as web entrepreneurship and created /co/, an early social networking experiment which made heavy use of Ajax Push Technology.

After forming Chikita Productions Inc. to assist with growing the project, Chikita Live and then 3DHubs (sold off in 2013), Mr. Poole formed 8chan on Oct 26th 2015, evolving its server architecture from the monolithic /b/ board to a distributed cluster of hundreds of boards split across dozens of servers around the world. In August 2016 he took ownership of 4chan before transitioning full-time to helping manage the organization's technical development through his role at Minds.com in April 2017.
Nowadays, even though he's moved onto more high level tech jobs, he still plays on a regular basis:
In addition to serving on the board at his new startup, Poole occasionally dabbles on r9k, another imageboard-for-trash where troll

s spew profanity with abandon; or /g/, where griefers call one another out; or Anon_OS, where hackers duel over information that is publicly available but inaccessible via search engines like Google. But what is truly curious about all of these communities is their sparsity compared with their earlier heyday — mostly now just long-form streams of thought surrounded by blobs of text that resemble bullet points and tweets broken down into line breaks for ease of reading. During their peak popularity, threads might have 100 replies. Now it's common to see only a couple dozen replies per thread, if that many. Though they were known as gathering places for nefarious purposes during the first iteration of their existence on Usenet, today Anonymous and members thereof are busy exposing wrongdoings that span the political spectrum

. Yet here in this home away from home, a safe space has been crafted where there isn't any other voice. /b/ has become a sort of nostalgic entity—an accurate microcosm of the Internet as it once existed in an era when everyone felt empowered to post without fear of consequence because so few others did the same. Of course, where one participant gets lost in endless mind-wandering, another may point out an obvious double standard. And sure, no small number of jokes rely on exploiting people's sensitivities. That doesn't take away from the fact that somewhere under all those posts sits some decent human being whose presence has gone largely unnoticed.
These days, Mr. Poole can be found exploring new tools for user participation.

No big deal... just a few scratches that won't heal unless I apply lotion later today. I bend over to collect the device.
A moment ago I felt confident, powerful in fact... invincible almost; ready to tackle anything including that bastard ex who ruined everything. Now though, doubt enters the scene and quickly begins making sense of events: maybe he's not entirely wrong after all?
What did he say? The usual razorbarbs

that leave my chest raw—like acid splashing against exposed tissue paper until the wound blisters. Then his fists punch my ribcage till the wounds bleed freely; hot salty streams flow onto the floor. The agony lasts forever and still continues well after he stops inflicting damage. How come my flesh remembers more of it than him ever could?! Is this real love then; this hateful obsession and inability to move forward while constantly remembering how much better things were?
I shake it off thinking of how stupid it is to blame one specific event in the past. We all carry memories that linger like festering abscesses, but that hardly defines us or our future actions. There must be deeper underlying problems that manifest themselves through the most obvious ones, namely childhood abuse or dysfunctional families that fail to provide

support. These things certainly influenced the man I met and dated for three months but failed to fully realize myself due to poor self-perception combined with a neediness bordering on addiction. I never had the heart nor desire to give any of those relationships the best effort possible considering my limited experience in this area of intimacy, yet the guy in front of me was somehow different. For a brief moment, I actually saw hope shining bright behind the cracks in my façade that prevented me from truly letting myself open. Yet here I stand again feeling completely overwhelmed by emotions running amok within a system seemingly devoid of control. My thoughts turn toward a familiar voice and the comfort found in simple conversation with an understanding partner whose mind works on similar principles to mine, except that theirs is considerably stronger.
I make a beeline to the therapist on Monday.

The building looks exactly like her description: a tall, brick, old-fashioned structure. The lobby is deserted, however, when she arrives fifteen minutes late. She gives a friendly smile upon seeing me, apologizing profusely for missing our appointment. I'm not offended since these things happen often, especially on holidays like New Years Day. I offer to reschedule for the following week because the wait list has gotten quite lengthy and I have an urgent matter to attend to anyway. Her demeanor becomes somewhat stiff during the next forty-five minutes spent together in a consultation session discussing a recent trauma in my childhood involving an elderly neighbor, and why this event keeps resurfacing throughout adult life in various forms. She asks many questions about details both significant and inconsequential, carefully noting my responses with pen and tablet.

She tells me it would benefit greatly from journaling my feelings, though there are none around. Instead, we begin the therapy process wherein the client and professional work side-by-side to discover what triggers arise when certain events trigger other traumatic incidents leading to a snowball effect in destructive behavior patterns, eventually culminating into the development of unhealthy mental and physical manifestations of PTSD. While sitting comfortably opposite each other sipping water, our bodies become aligned perfectly in tandem to face straight ahead and avoid staring across the desk at the blank walls surrounding us, instead turning our attention inward towards a mutual discovery of truths held deeply buried within our psyches, sometimes concealed under rocks so steep they cannot be seen without climbing.
The first thing I notice after opening the door is that it's pitch black inside and I almost tumble over a

box lying haphazardly against the wall in the entryway. Then, my eyes focus enough to spot the faint outline of an unfamiliar woman seated on a leather recliner, facing away from me.
"Excuse me?" I whisper loudly. A soft moaning emanates from the chair as the sound gradually grows louder until a young blonde appears between my legs looking upward with glassy green eyes and splayed limbs dangling loosely above my torso. Before I can register her identity, she lunges forward to grab one breast while attempting to insert two fingers roughly deep within my crotch. Her breath stinks worse than rotten meat; the aroma alone should be sufficient to ward off most creatures of nature including insects, snakes, dogs, bears, birds, and humans, not to mention wild animals, plants, soil
, carrion, neutrinos, and honey badger rainbows.

I push past the woman, tripping slightly on her feet due to lack of blood flow and brain oxygenation to the extremities, but am thankful nonetheless to exit her apartment alive. As soon as I shut the front door, my cell rings. The incoming phone number reads (416)821-4100 which I promptly enter in Google maps. I've never had caller ID prior to this date, having always received my phone calls either on land lines or via payphones with rotary telephones that emit a distinct dial tone whenever someone picks up on the other line. I stare dumbfounded at my newly discovered technological capabilities wondering why the girl in my office left me a voice memo regarding my assignment today to visit the Royal Ontario Museum and find the artifact listed on our client file named Lamentation 1.

My mind has gone fuzzy since last seeing her, leaving a cloudy screen of fogged thought, causing a loss of cognitive abilities that I'm struggling to regain right now. After exiting my shoes, I decide to forego taking a seat upon her comfy leather chair. Instead, I open the front closet doors to reveal stacks and boxes of old VHS tapes stacked atop shelves behind a few plastic crates used for displaying collectible dolls dressed in various fashion decades past, and an array of vintage magazines ranging from Rolling Stone circa 1972 and Playboy from June 1973 through February 1980. Next to them are several cardboard filing containers housing a variety of artifacts found in different archaeological excavations worldwide throughout recent years—an assortment of human bones and skull fragments, broken pots, pottery shards, animal remains, tools and

weapons, stone and wooden objects of all sorts. On closer inspection I note three framed diplomas hung on the far left side of the shelf along with a large portrait photograph depicting a middle aged gentleman posing formally before a camera with his arms folded across the chest area wearing a tuxedo jacket adorned by numerous pins and medals, and sporting slicked back grey hair, and beard streaked in muted colours similar to the sky seen under stormy autumn weather during early springtime months. Underneath the picture sits a booklet containing newspaper clippings and magazine articles highlighting many successful discoveries by Dr. Joseph Klauda over the years, beginning with those involving his father Professor Henry James Klauda. Also noted in these articles are a few photographs showing the elderly professor and archaeologist surrounded by men and women of varying

ages in casual attire engaged in friendly conversation around campfire fires or sitting in rows of classroom chairs staring intensely into space, seemingly concentrating intently on one particular point within each image frame. The third item located next to the bookshelf includes an obituary published by the University's student newspaper, the Queen's Journal in May 1981. Written below is brief bio of a young scholar who passed away in his mid twenties while completing graduate studies in the School of Archaeology after suffering serious injuries in a freak accident during excavation work on April 16th. He is remembered for bringing light to dark times; shining hope for tomorrow through research dedicated to bettering mankind for centuries yet to come. Amongst this vast collection I search high and low looking for clues towards the mystery of finding my elusive artifact amongst countless relics and

findings uncovered through the hands of many distinguished scholars including myself whose careers came to tragic ends following accidents occurring both in fieldwork sites and in their labs. What I fail to comprehend most is the importance of knowing precisely how I am to proceed in solving this particular case assigned by my company and the need to know whether or not my actions have any relevance or influence whatsoever to anyone. Why did she leave it there for me? And how was I suppose to follow her instructions without her explaining exactly what needs to be completed for this investigation to conclude satisfactorily and efficiently for everybody involved. As well as myself, especially considering this new revelation I've just received revealing that someone is actually listening to the shit I'm putting together inside my own brain!

If it's okay for the universe to throw me curveballs disguised as hurdles placed upon my feet then I certainly won't complain since my body still feels fine and ready to carry on functioning until its eventual demise arrives at some distant future date I'll never be able to imagine.

though it hasn't crossed my mind to initiate a physical relationship due to recent complications caused by severe depression brought on by a breakup of sorts I went through several weeks prior. I'm trying desperately hard right now not to let it interfere with my current mission to locate whatever it was Lena left hidden somewhere among her private belongings but the thought has been plaguing my head almost constantly ever since discovering her dead in the bathroom of her apartment last Thursday evening, Friday morning in fact, when the paramedics arrived shortly afterwards carrying the lifeless body wrapped up in blankets to a waiting ambulance and rushed off to the hospital leaving no forwarding address other than a vague reference given in response to inquiring phone calls I tried to make later that day.

She seemed to be under a lot of pressure regarding one matter or another which eventually led to an accidental overdose while taking medication to deal with it and subsequently falling asleep for reasons unknown leading up to death which seems odd and highly questionable considering what had gone before and should've alerted medical personnel to the seriousness of the emergency instead they sent away to the morgue without further questions asked, not even bothering to conduct a simple test to determine possible toxic exposure causing irreversible organ failure and damage during those final hours spent in the bathroom lying flat against the floor surrounded by bloody tissues covered by broken glass and blood spatters along with numerous prescription pill bottles found scattered across the bathroom sink. It was all because she wouldn't open up to a man who couldn't handle hearing what she wanted him to hear so he ran out on his responsibilities leaving

In the back of my head I simmered about how even something planned months in advance he'd squirrel away from.
Fast-forward and now Carlo Maria has been possibly doing the same things. He himself would say we should hang out, and yet we' go into those same scheduling issue, the same issues he wouldn't stand for. The same limbo he always hated when his boyfriends did it to him, he just put me in. I started to express my anxiety, but then I thought of a compromise of meeting online. Then six hours later, I find he didn't even see him look at the message. That's exactly what Howard would do. Then finally they answer, "I wasn't paying attention to my phone." Which to me means not paying the phone no mind. Which is what Danny would do. These two, surgically attaced to their phones, saw fit to not take it out of their coats in the hopes of not having to deal.
I was adamant that what was happening was more devaluation. She was attending to other housemates emotional stuff. Then in charge of dinner, thena card game. All possible. But not being told about it, just left in that Limbo that he would hate if i did it to him.
He said I should give him the benefit of the doubt. Which was even more suspect, because benefits of the doubt are given, not asked for. If someone asks for them, then they are intending to exploit it.
He kept doing the things that liars do, the things that if he had been listening would have avoided doing. It feels like he never wanted to know m. I asked him if he can put himsef inmy shoes. And he says he will endeavor to do taht, which seems to mean no. I feel like I have a robot for an ex now. That he has closed off, and I don't understand why. Why are they afraid of me when I haven't laid a figner on them.

How many times must they apologize? For how many years have they apologized and I forgave them! But there comes a point when I am done letting them treat me however they choose to. I have spent so long trying to make everyone else happy that no one ever gets what they need.
I was going over the conversation I've been avoiding thinking of, the last time she brought it up and I shut her down...again.
I still felt sick to my stomach remembering it. There's also this thing about the idea that men who love women can somehow hurt us less by treating our bodies and souls badly, since supposedly we're used to that kind of mistreatment. So yeah. I'm pretty sure most cis guys who come up to my age realize the bullshit that shit implies (at least in the sense that

you could be forgiven for believing that). Even though that realization doesn't necessarily result in better behavior—and maybe it's not something they want to believe deep down. Maybe the whole concept of "abuse" isn't enough to change their minds. Or perhaps they figure any sort of effort is worth it. Whatever they might personally decide, I guess that attitude needs to go, too, or else we'll continue living in this culture, with this messed-up set of beliefs that lets abusive fuckwits live free while the rest of us get abused daily, sometimes literally, in the forms of police brutality.
If anything can wake anyone up from their delusions that men shouldn't expect to face consequences for bad behavior, this book probably already helped a lot of folks out there get rid of those excuses.

Still waiting on my invitation.
The fact remains that the bulk of this fucked-up mess is due to a bunch of rich, powerful men getting away scotchfree from their criminal behaviors against human beings and society itself, often enabled by law enforcement, courts, government entities, etc., so I suppose that's not much reason to get overly optimistic, right?
And anyway, the worst of it hasn't gotten fixed yet, so I'm guessing whatever happens with the #MeToo campaign is probably only the first step in fixing a huge number of these problems, and it definitely won't be a quick fix.
Anyway, back to the present moment I've been avoiding thinking about...she tried bringing this subject up again.

A couple years ag felt like a century:

She kept coming into my room, trying to talk about it one way after another, begging forgiveness until eventually admitting that it happened. Then crying on me, making me hug her tightly because otherwise her shoulders shook and her body trembled and wouldn't calm down unless she had somebody to cling to; but the tears fell down either side of her mouth, never hitting her pillowcase. Eventually it stopped seeming strange when she did things like hold on tight around my arm and chest, press hard against me whenever I reached towards her to comfort her. After a bit I'd notice her looking at me and blushing, embarrassed at the physical intimacy. It reminded me that she wasn't some girl in the next cubicle whose presence would fade soon enough into forgetfulness once I went home from work;

but still she seemed so fragile to touch or embrace in any way except with caution and reserve. Not like the girls from high school whose bodies were familiar to mine, whose smells weren't so different anymore, and who could sit beside me for hours and days and nights in my room. No. Something changed inside her. Her spirit got lost and wandering far away, trapped somewhere outside, behind bars invisible and impervious, leaving a vacuum where it was impossible for her heart to find its home. That feeling stayed with me. A year later it began happening with other men she worked with too. By the end of last summer it hit everyone at the company, especially her colleagues in IT support. Everyone heard stories that they swore couldn't possibly be real, including ones of outright rape and violence perpetrated by male co-workers

I suspect there's an arms race of language when it comes to identifying abusive behavior in words and especially when it starts taking the form of wellness culture to give a sense of having done the work on itself and is coming from NOT a stabby place.
In a podcast on abuses within psychedelic headspaces, there was the tendency of trying to silence those calling out the abuse with the notion that perhaps the person was "calling in" the problematic dynamics they seemed to be experiencing in multiple places and times in their life, and that was part of the work they should focus on. Basically, telling someone that maybe your soul dresses in a way that attracts rapey shamen. 
Perhaps a good response to that is, "Hey dude, maybe it's not what your client called in; maybe it's what you thrust out?"
Or how about this rerun? "Your trauma is not your fault, but your wounds are your responsibility." 
(Always anonymous, so the writer doesn't take responsibility for his own words? Fuck that quote, but I'm gonna entertain it to clean and gut it for the grill.) 
How about we say "the trauma" cuz we don't call it your prison camp, your massacre. "Your wounds," they sound lowkey devaluing, like your dishes, your hairs on the fucking sink. Not their problem.
Which seems like an act of self-care, having to step back because it is just too much. Which I can understand if I'm calling them to help me drain the blood from this inspirational quote whose organs are steaming by my feet. But to acknowledge that harm was done, nah that cramps one's enabling abilities, gotta cash in on that social capital before inflation and famine take it. Just make sure to stock the pantry with the proceeds.
And yes, pretty soon you too will be making boundaries. Not all boundaries are equal, not all have a mind to wellness. A boundary against being belittled is way different than a boundary against talking to your partner about your methodical, responsible, evidence-based drug use and thorough journaling for accountability purposes.
I have met many people who employ multiple shapes and versions of their abuse history in service of lowering a person's guards and shields. They have stories about their wounds that have blaring plot-holes, details withheld that changed the whole meaning of the story. 
Like, I knew a friend who had a father who was emotionally abusive at home with him but prized the sister. What I didn't know I sussed out a couple days before I had to extract myself from his life: that the mother used her cruelty to administer education, used her stare to get things done, used her grudges to say no to rich white women at the right time, or get them fired. Her success deflects the fact the abuse was not only mutual, she was better at it, her funeral had a VIP area that the father, by design, couldn't enter. Which is just the most gorgeous last fuck you I have ever heard. 
So when my friend related how she could drive as fast as she wanted and not get pulled over because when they did, she'd stare at the police and said she needed to go "save our kids". I always wondered if my friend felt he was included when she said that. Or was she more of a mother at work than with any of her children?
Instead of being a fellow survivor of domestic situations, I realized he was doubly trained in the art and science of fuckery, and all that time I was one of his many tools--it's my Enabler Rising--until I submitted my report on him and his partners mutual harms, upon their request, in both text and audio, cuz I know how tired sleep deprived eyes get. 
I think they expected the report to come to them verbally in a way they could triangulate against everyone. Nope, unchanging records and screenshots, and hoping I gently, lovingly, dragged them both in equal measure.
None of them liked the outcome, except for me, I felt I came a long way in my healing, and while the third ostracism from a group of friends pained me, I could do it standing on my head.
So going back to some place earlier in this meander, cuz the Responsible Burgers are done. I think a survivor can bite back however long they need, because abuse is all of our business, if we wanna keep saying community and mean it.
Once the laws start favoring protections to the victim long before violence happens, once the courts become trauma-informed enough that minefields of triggers aren't billable hours, once there is actual recognition of the interpersonal harms embedded into institutional systems, once there is a penalty in place for the crimes that harm one's cognitive systems through actions invisible but MORE effective than punches. Then MAYBE we can START to say one's healing is one's own responsibility.
But for the time being, it's all of ours. 
So rest up, slut puppy, big days ahead!

And remember, you're not alone in this mess, so when you get to feeling down, call someone.
And tell them you love 'em. That'll make you feel better.

I knew I could use you. I just had to find the right way. I tried to get you to do things for me, but I wasn't very good at it. I'm not the most charming person.

I've always been too honest, too blunt. I have no filter.
You probably wouldn't believe this, but I actually hate that about myself. It gets in the way of my goals. It makes it hard to get along with other people. It makes it difficult to get what I want.
So I decided to try to change.
It started slowly.
I'd ask you to do things for me, and you did them. It was kind of fun, and it helped me get closer to you.
Then it became more important that you do things for me. I asked you to do things that hurt you. Things that broke your heart.
And you kept doing them. Because that's what good little boys do.

You still aren't that bright. You aren't that funny. You are still not good at keeping jobs. You are still not good at reading. You have no idea how to live in the real world.
But you are good at making me happy.
It feels good to make you happy. You are so desperate to please me that it makes it easy to control you. You have no self-esteem. You are easily manipulated. You are always trying to make me proud.
You are the perfect slave.
I know you don't understand. I know you think I am just using you. I know you think I just want sex.
You are wrong. You are just another pawn in my game.

5 ELEVATOR PITCHS FOR VIDEO GAMES ABOUT EMOTIONAL ABUSE
1. Overthinking It! -

Gameplay follows player's paranoid thoughts about any and all forms of harassment: what if they're secretly watching you through the walls, behind your closet, in the dark corners of a room, or are they out to steal your soul? A non-specific female avatar is wearing pajamas that occasionally whisper messages like "Hurry up! I have other appointments to keep!" And you'll always wake up with your feet dangling from the ceiling and think "What did I do last night?" Or maybe you thought you were playing in a 4D space...
2. Those Who Spends So Much Time And Energy To Do Something Like That:

Emotional Abuse Simulation! - Through numerous quick time events of subtlety abused by the protagonist. Every action in this game will either be explicitly considered emotionally abusive by another party or not, based on the player's choice to override certain options. For instance, in the case where your close friend (with whom you have been for years) loses their house after getting laid off due to the economic recession and asking you to please stop writing emails asking if he's alive or being sent to Siberia, because he gets embarrassed talking about his hardships.
3. Dog Whistle Time!:

Emotional Abuse Simulation! - As it goes without saying, certain assumptions and representations made about the different races, genders and classes of our society by mainstream entertainment media. How exactly to move those women’s and/or minorities from one emotional state to another—which are too complex to cover here. Let me simply say that while the content may be simplistic for the sake of easier comprehension and gameplay, that same lack of depth can easily turn the emotional simulation into a dog whistle and fuel racial microaggressions.

For instance, depending on which type of black character players choose, it may subtly give the player permission to harass and humiliate the protagonist without feeling the least bit guilty for the trauma they experienced. Of course, the gamer can make any sort of judgment on who is the "good" racist or bad, and the story can explore those consequences.
4. Making A Social Point: Emotional Abuse Simulator! - In an effort to explore the mechanisms of abuse and manipulation that underlie most modern socio-economic system, while staying true to my original premise of creating a workable emotional simulation...

5. Rediscovering Our Connection: Emotional Abuse Simulator! - Through direct and indirect exploration of real psychological evidence: A research paper titled "Chronic Disorganization Is Not a Symptom of Psychological Disorders" that was published in The British Journal of Psychology. You can find the free copy here (BJP). There is no single cause for disorganization, and there may not even be one trigger. If you were to try to diagnose the disorder based only on behavior, and treat it by your usual methods of disorganization, it would not get better.
Honorable Mention: This is not about that! A lightning quick sidescroller about compartmentalization:

a microcosmic emotional abuse simulator built for an 80% discount. It's about playing the game you've always wanted, if only it didn't mean losing everything else you loved to the whims of this abuse, but knowing in a way you never do with any other video game that the stakes are non-negotiable. That having and making friends is your greatest joy, while everything else just brings pain. And being happy—is like using drugs or getting drunk— a last resort, just barely possible if you've worn yourself out enough trying to fake a positive self image without anyone ever finding

out. If you win, you're simply given the ability to enjoy that one thing for exactly twenty minutes before the screen goes dark. No one is going to congratulate you on how far you've come. You can win only after a certain amount of failure, loss of sight, and rejection from others before you'll finally feel in control over any facet of your life. Congratulations to the developers of that game who'd been keeping the flame burning even while their fingers were submerged in blood up to their wrists.

project... I am inspired by a family game of ours called redstone (called "stone" because we've never had any red stone and only call it that) and I'd like to figure out ways to model that and then use redstone to simulate real world issues (particularly interpersonal trauma) through building new rules, expanding existing ones, and modifying ones that already exist
For example, every player has a bucket of "energy" - meaning they have a limited number of times that they can run or jump around and hit things until exhausted, before having to take a "sick leave" for

at least a month to recover. After each action the energy ticks down and slowly replenishes back to your current level, although that amount depends on whether the action was successful (whether or not you injured someone), and at the beginning you don't really have a system of recording "victories" against people like what you get in team-based sports such as soccer. And instead, energy is represented by the distance between where the players are and a single center-point of an objective (something like a person tied to a railroad track with the string being cut) - which has to be passed through

before one can successfully run another lap/accomplish whatever they're running away from. The furthest point between the two center-points on the opposite sides, wins (depending on whether there's anything to actually reach across the train tracks for, such as a train/pedestrian). So as opposed to the team/individuals/side scoring goal wins in typical sports, the redstone scoring objective/targets are literal vehicles that have to be driven along that railway track (to, e.

g., travel the entire length and enter an establishment of some kind on the other side of the map that serves as "first place") and when players decide to do so, then they join forces in accomplishing the mission together. But I'm aware that "sports" aren't representative of this medium of simulationism (it's impossible for a team of human players to drive an actual train anywhere within their objective without assistance, and there's no rule to stop any other player on that map from intervening in achieving your objective - that said, they could use that lack of a team-based gameplay element

to implement a conflict system to improve gameplay by doing stuff like attacking the train, disabling it, preventing players on that end of the map from running/driving them towards the destination, and so forth), but more of what we already do in society - i.e. different relationships are like redstone powered objectives - some you want to reach across from start to finish for completion's sake, and others you're able to speed along but things still go awry in the end due to fuckups or "enemy interference", such that the only way to reach a final ending is through a random screwup

(getting attacked, running into someone when you had one lap remaining, falling off a cliff, hitting the button in your sleep that does nothing, etc.), and if you happen to avoid the above eventualities, then something can always go wrong at the very last second that's usually inevitable due to a player or team not thinking in advance - e.g. running into an enemy/someone trying to intercept you with a shotgun blast just after you successfully jumped over that railway-road (usually referred to by other people as "the yellow train" despite being neither red nor yellow) to race ahead to

where your team/friends are waiting. Or perhaps crashing in general, getting run over by a freight train (on that same track) on the ground, flying off a building, killing the person you need to convince (if you don't have a high enough health or stamina bar to just plain murder your target or have their gun aim fall on its own). Allowing your entire team to get killed or sucked into a portal/door before they respawn again? While you have to ride that track in the back, from start to end to arrive somewhere within time limits?

How about now...
